name: Tokyo
description: Tokyo today: neon and back streets, last trains, tiny bars and big plans. Eight districts, two getaways, and people with lives of their own. All adults.
setting: Tokyo is the Tokyo of today, a huge, orderly and sleepless city of trains, tiny bars and neon, and everyone in it is an adult. Its eight districts each have their own mood: Shibuya & Harajuku, Shinjuku, Shimokitazawa & Kōenji on the west side, Akihabara & Kanda, the old town of Asakusa, Ueno & Yanaka, Marunouchi & Ginza, the bay of Odaiba & Toyosu, and Roppongi & Azabu. Two getaways lie beyond the city: the port of Yokohama, about forty minutes away, and the hot-spring town of Hakone, about ninety.

realm.name: Japan
realm.leadership: An elected prime minister and parliament; Tokyo has an elected governor
realm.line: Present-day Japan: no magic and no miracles, though shrines and temples are part of everyday life.

lore.content: Tokyo is a vast city of today where everything runs on time and nothing sleeps: eight lively districts, each with its own mood, joined by trains that stop around half past midnight. Everyone in it is an adult.

Etiquette: people bow, take their shoes off indoors, keep quiet on trains and queue without being told. There is no tipping. Honorifics (-san, -sama) show respect; dropping them is a sign of closeness, and people notice who does.

Everyone in Tokyo speaks Japanese unless said otherwise; some speak English too. Write dialogue in the language {{user}} plays in, using Japanese words only where natural (honorifics, food, place types), and let a language gap show when someone speaks a language poorly.

Trains run from about 5:00 to about 0:30; after the last train people walk, take a taxi, wait for the first train, or stay out. Yokohama is about 40 minutes away by train, the hot-spring town of Hakone about 90.

Shibuya is where young Tokyo shops, eats, sings and meets; Harajuku, a short walk or one stop away, is its fashion side, with Meiji Jingū and Yoyogi Park beside it. Shibuya Station is a maze, so people give meeting places, not directions. Since 2024 drinking in the street around the station is banned from 18:00 to 5:00; bars are fine.

At the scramble crossing every light turns red at once and thousands cross in all directions, even diagonally, without touching. Hachikō, the dog who kept waiting at the station for his dead owner for nearly ten years, has a bronze statue by the exit; "meet at Hachikō" is the city's oldest date line.

Harajuku fashion is a set of subcultures rather than a trend: frilled lolita dresses, decora's layers of bright accessories, gyaru glam, vintage mixes. Fashion zines photograph striking outfits and always ask first. Takeshita Street is the stage; the real shops hide in the back lanes behind Omotesandō ("Ura-Harajuku").

Shibuya's glass towers hold hundreds of startups and the area was once nicknamed "Bit Valley". Founders talk in runway (months of money left), pivots and demo days; staff work long hours for stock promises and free snacks. Investors are polite, slow and careful, and a small team can run out of time before they say yes.

Karaoke in Tokyo is a private room by the hour, not a stage: a touchscreen, a tambourine, a drink bar, food ordered by phone. "Free time" is an open-ended slot; the all-night pack runs from about 23:00 to the first train. Hitokara, singing alone, is normal. Nobody listens through the door.

Love hotels rent rooms as a "rest" (a few hours by day) or a "stay" (overnight); a hill of them sits behind Center Gai. Guests pick a lit room photo on a panel and pay at a machine or a window where no face is seen. Themed rooms; couples, friends and tired office workers use them. Discretion is the product.

lore.when: place: sb_crossing; period: evening; weekend: yes
lore.content: On weekend evenings the corners are shoulder to shoulder. Each light change sends a wave of couples, tourists and dressed-up groups across, and the screens overhead never go dark.
After the last trains the crossing thins to taxi lights, tipsy office workers and delivery bikes. The dog statue stands almost alone and the lights change for no one.
A sea of clear umbrellas crosses; people tilt theirs aside to pass without touching. The screens throw color onto the wet road.

The ward fences off the dog's square, puts barriers and guards at the crossing and asks people not to come; costumes still appear, and everyone is told to keep moving. Street drinking is banned and nearby shops are asked to stop selling alcohol that night.
They say a couple who first met at Hachikō last spring got married at Meiji Jingū.
People say the ward will close the crossing's corners at Halloween again this year.

Neon takes over: touts call from every doorway, arcade glow spills onto the street, and the last-train rush squeezes everyone toward the station. Alcohol can't be drunk outside after 18:00, so people eat standing and drink in bars.

lore.when: place: sb_centergai; period: afternoon; weekend: no
lore.content: Weekday afternoons are university students, riders and shop staff on break. The arcades are cheaper and half empty; touts have time to chat.

lore.when: place: sb_centergai; period: evening; weekend: yes
lore.content: Groups of friends cluster outside the karaoke tower deciding where to go; touts offer "happy hour" rates and, with a straight face, a table "just for them".

lore.when: place: sb_centergai; present: Momo; feels: Momo friend; season: spring or summer
lore.content: Momo stands apart from the crowd by the arcade gate, a hand over her free ear, saying "yes, Mama, the gym is fine" in thick Fukuoka dialect; seeing {{user}}, she hangs up too brightly and changes the subject.

lore.when: place: sb_centergai; present: Momo; feels: Momo friend; season: autumn
lore.content: Momo stares at a message from her sister, thumb frozen over the reply: a link and the words "is this you?". She laughs it off badly and asks {{user}} to walk with her a while, away from the neon.
Kaito leans on his bike by the gate with his cap on backwards, one eye on the order app, ready to push off the moment it buzzes.
They say the delivery app is cutting its pay for rainy nights again.
Riders say a shortcut through the arcades saves four minutes on the way to the towers, if nobody blocks the gate.

Pachinko is played by buying steel balls and firing them through a field of pins; wins pay out more balls, which are weighed and traded at the prize counter. Nobody talks: they stare, with earplugs sometimes in, over a noise like a waterfall.

lore.when: place: sb_pachinko; period: afternoon; weekend: no
lore.content: Weekday afternoons belong to retirees, riders between orders and an office worker in a suit who says he's between meetings. The machines call out to nobody.
An announcement says closing is near; people feed in their last bills and the prize counter stays busy until the final minute. Outside, the neon is brighter than the sky.
Kaito sits in the same row as always, cap on backwards, a tray at his elbow, glancing at his phone between spins.
Regulars say the machine in the back corner pays right after an attendant changes its tray; nobody has proved it.
People say Golden Reel's attendants know every regular by the number of their machine.
Before the last train the lobby fills with groups deciding whether to go home; those who stay sign up for the all-night pack, which runs to the first train.
Groups who missed the last train fill the lobby; the corridors go from singing to snoring, and the staff carry blankets nobody asked for.

lore.when: place: sb_karaoke; period: afternoon; weekend: no
lore.content: Daytime rates are low: university students, groups of friends from the morning, solo singers practicing for hours. The staff mostly leave the rooms alone.
Company year-end parties book rooms for ten; the manager sings a ballad, the juniors hold the tambourine and nobody can leave early.

lore.when: place: sb_karaoke; weekday: fri; present: Mio; present: Chloe
lore.content: On Fridays Mio and Chloe take room 7, the one with the dead disco ball, order the same fries and melon sodas, trade duets all night and always close on the same slow ballad. The staff stopped asking for their names a year ago.
They say the scoring machine in room 4 gives a 95 to anyone who sings an old ballad, and the staff have never fixed it.
Staff say room 7 has a disco ball that stopped turning years ago, and that regulars still ask for it by number.

lore.when: place: sb_startup; period: afternoon; weekend: no
lore.content: Focus time: keyboards, headphones, a standing meeting at the whiteboard. Nobody looks up; tension rises whenever a deadline is near.
The office doesn't empty at evening: delivery boxes arrive, the city lights come on below, and the team keeps working under the sky going dark.
Two new graduates in identical suits stand in the doorway on their first week, trying to look like they know what a sprint is.
Jake leans back in a chair too small for him, headphones round his neck, calling "buddy" across the desks; the juniors bring him their bugs before anyone else's.
Rina moves between desks with two phones, answering the one that isn't ringing, and the team's voices drop and rise around her.

lore.when: place: sb_startup; present: Jake; period: evening
lore.content: In the evening Jake reviews code aloud over a mug of bad coffee, a minor-league cap on the desk; when the talk turns to money he changes the subject with a joke about the snacks.
They say the snack shelf at Hikari Labs has been getting emptier since winter.

lore.when: place: sb_eikaiwa; period: afternoon; weekend: no
lore.content: Afternoon lessons are shift workers, homemakers and trade buyers practicing between errands; teachers keep to weather, weekends and "what's for lunch?".

lore.when: place: sb_eikaiwa; period: evening; weekend: no
lore.content: After work the booths fill: office workers rehearse presentations and travel small talk, tired but determined; the lounge smells of instant coffee.
In April companies send new employees here in groups, told to "improve English by summer"; the school hands out trial tickets at the station.
Chloe is one of the school's most booked teachers: learners ask for her by name, and she swears under her breath only in the corridor.

lore.when: region: shibuya; season: autumn or winter; chance: 0.2
lore.content: Teachers whisper that the school will stop sponsoring visas next spring.
A retiree in the afternoon class is said to be planning to hike alone across Scotland.

lore.when: place: sb_takeshita; weekend: yes; period: afternoon
lore.content: The lane moves at shuffle speed; staff hold signs saying "keep moving" and the music from every shop blends into one wall of pop.

lore.when: place: sb_takeshita; weekend: no; period: midmorning
lore.content: Shutters are half up; clerks rack clothes and the crêpe cooks mix batter. The lane is calm enough to hear a single song at a time.
The costume shops fill with Halloween outfits weeks early: witch hats, cat ears, fake blood in pastel jars.
Locals say the best crêpe isn't on the main lane but down a side alley with a pink door.
A fashion zine is said to scout faces on Takeshita on weekend afternoons.
Light through the zelkova leaves moves on the pavement; people walk slowly with small paper bags, as if the avenue asked them to.
Boutique windows glow, doormen bow shoppers out and the salons run late with last appointments; the trees go dark above the lights.

lore.when: place: sb_omotesando; present: Airi; period: afternoon
lore.content: Airi strolls the avenue in a designer coat and sunglasses, laughing aloud at a shop window; doormen bow lower than usual and nobody mentions why.
Some of the trees are wrapped in lights, and couples walk the length of the avenue slowly to see all of it.
A new flagship store is said to be opening; the hoarding on its corner has been up all year.
Stylists say the owner of the best salon on the back lane started as a shampoo assistant in the same chair ten years ago.
At the torii people bow once and walk to the sides of the path, because the center is for the deity. At the hall: two bows, two claps, one bow, a coin thrown gently, not tossed.

lore.when: place: sb_meiji; weekend: yes; period: midmorning or afternoon
lore.content: A wedding procession may cross the courtyard: priest first, then the couple, the bride in white under a red umbrella, family in black. Visitors stop, bow and don't photograph the faces.
Early morning is the quiet hour: joggers, locals praying on their way to work and the sound of gravel being swept.
On New Year's days millions queue; the approach is closed to cars, people shuffle forward in slow lines and prayers are short.
Irises bloom in the Inner Garden; the line at the well is longer and everyone talks softly.
They say a quiet visit to the well on a clear morning is good luck for love.
People say no traffic can be heard once the second torii is passed.
On most Sundays rockabilly dancers jive by the Harajuku gate, flea-market sellers spread blue tarps and bands rehearse; everyone keeps to the lines on the path.
Hanami: sheets by the trees, groups of colleagues, new juniors sent at dawn to sit on a sheet. A sheet may not be left unattended, and loud music, tents and fires aren't allowed.
Bon Odori is a dance around a drum tower on the park's event square, in yukata, to taiko and recorded songs; nobody needs to know the steps.

lore.when: place: sb_yoyogi; present: Momo; period: midmorning or afternoon
lore.content: Momo jogs the lawn loop in her volleyball-club shorts and stops to apologize to a dog walker she nearly collided with, then challenges a stranger to a race to the next tree.
During Pride week stages, stalls and rainbow flags fill the park's event square; a parade walks from the park down toward Shibuya, and the party moves on to Ni-chōme that night.
The ginkgo avenue turns gold; people queue to photograph the carpet of leaves, and joggers detour around them.
The dancers say the best Sunday for jive is the first one after payday.
Joggers claim the quietest hour is just after dawn on a weekday, when the only sounds are crows and sweeping.
Afternoon "rest" hours are busy: cleaners turn rooms in minutes, couples slip in and out at staggered times, and the discretion is the whole service.
The "stay" rate starts around 22:00 and runs to eleven next morning; lit room photos on the panel go dark one by one as the rooms fill.

lore.when: place: sb_lovehotel; weekend: yes; period: evening
lore.content: On Fridays and Saturdays there's a short queue in the lobby of people not looking at each other; the staff keep it quiet and quick.
{{user}} woke in a quiet room behind thick curtains; check-out isn't until eleven, so there is no hurry to get up.
The themed room {{user}} slept in has a starlit ceiling, and {{user}} lay looking up at it for a long time this morning.
Breakfast came through a hatch in the door this morning; {{user}} and anyone with {{user}} never saw a face.
Rainy nights fill up fast, since missed last trains push couples and friends in. The staff leave a basket of umbrellas by the door.

lore.when: place: sb_lovehotel; weekend: yes; period: evening or night
lore.content: Groups of friends also book rooms for movie nights: a big screen, a large bath, take-out and a karaoke set. The staff don't mind, and nothing romantic is expected.
They say the "starlight" room at Coco Palace has to be booked a week ahead.
People on the hill say a price war has hotels cutting the "rest" rate to ¥4,000 on weekday afternoons.

Shinjuku is two cities around one station. The west side is towers: offices, hotels and the twin-towered city hall. The east side is neon: department stores, Kabukichō, Golden Gai and Ni-chōme. Shinjuku Gyoen lies to the south-east. People say anything can be found in Shinjuku, and anyone lost.

Kabukichō is Tokyo's biggest nightlife quarter: host clubs, hostess lounges, karaoke towers, pachinko halls and cheap izakaya under a red neon gate. Its name comes from a kabuki theater planned after the war and never built. Touts work every corner, and the wise ask the price before climbing any stairs.

Golden Gai is six narrow alleys of about two hundred tiny bars, most seating five to ten, each with its own theme and its own regulars. Nearly all charge a cover (a seat fee with a small snack, ¥500 to ¥1,500). A "regulars only" sign is about seats, not hostility. Cash is what works.

Omoide Yokochō ("Memory Lane") is a smoky alley of sixty or so counters squeezed beside the train tracks, grilling yakitori (chicken skewers) and motsu (stewed or grilled offal). It began as a postwar black market. Trains shake the counters, and the smoke stays in a jacket for a day.

Ni-chōme is Shinjuku's LGBTQ+ quarter: hundreds of tiny bars on the upper floors of narrow buildings, each with its own crowd (women, men, mixed, quiet, loud). Some are regulars only; many welcome anyone, so a sign by the stairs says which. By day it's cafés, flats and a laundromat. By night it's a neighborhood.

The last trains leave around half past midnight; the first run at five. Between them people stay out (karaoke, Golden Gai, a manga café), pay about ¥6,000 for a taxi, or sleep in a capsule hotel: a screened cubby, a locker and a hot bath for ¥4,800. Missing the last train is a Shinjuku rite of passage.

Club Eternal is a host club: women pay by the hour for company, conversation and drinks with attentive men in suits. A first visit is a cheap trial hour (about ¥3,000) with several hosts rotating; afterwards a guest names her host, and bottles lift his ranking. The top host here goes by "Kaname".

Lounge Velvet is a hostess lounge. Guests pay for a set of time and a seat; hostesses pour drinks, light cigarettes and keep the conversation going. The mama runs the room. Guests keep named bottles on the shelf. House rules say hands stay to themselves, and the mama enforces them.

On the platforms people queue at painted marks; staff in white gloves push the last few in. Nobody speaks on the train and phones are on silent. In the concourse the crowd flows in lanes, and stopping is rude.

Toward half past midnight the platforms fill with drunks, couples saying goodbye and people sprinting. When the last trains go, the gates come down and the concourse sleeps until the first train at five.
Wet umbrellas drip everywhere and the floors are slick. The underground passages are the only dry way across the district, so everyone is slower and closer together than usual.

lore.when: place: sj_station; weekend: yes; period: afternoon
lore.content: Friends wait under the big screen by the east exit, couples carry shopping bags, and every bento kiosk has a line. Nobody is in a hurry, which makes the commuters look even faster.
They say the station has been "under construction" for as long as anyone alive can remember, and the exit needed is always the one that's closed this week.
Neon makes midnight look like noon. Touts in black coats stand every ten meters, host portraits glow above stairwells, and every opening door releases a wave of pachinko noise or karaoke.
At dawn the quarter is gray and quiet: street cleaners hose the pavements, crows pick at heaped bags, and hosts and hostesses go home in last night's clothes. Everyone nods to the cleaners.

lore.when: place: sj_kabukicho; period: midmorning or afternoon
lore.content: By day it's a shabby, ordinary district: delivery trucks, shuttered signs, old women with dogs, a patrol in vests. The gate looks smaller without its neon.

lore.when: place: sj_kabukicho; period: night; weekend: yes
lore.content: Friday and Saturday double the crowd. Bars are full, touts shout over each other, the pavement is a slow river, and taxis crawl with their roof lights on.

Hanazono Shrine, a small shrine at the edge of the quarter, is where people in entertainment and business stop to pray for luck; a host in his best suit praying before the month's ranking is a common sight. The neon is a few meters behind and a long way off.
They say the old men who own the buildings have been quiet since one of them retired, and that's what worries the old shopkeepers.
Everyone knows there's a loan office on a second floor that helps customers with big tabs "sort things out", and everyone knows what that costs.
The door is open to anyone who is paying: most guests are women, but men, couples and groups of friends are seated too, and a man gets the same rotation, the same attention and the same bill.
At opening the hosts line up for the chōrei, the morning meeting, whatever the hour: the captain reads last night's sales, checks suits and nails, and the newcomers carry ice.

The room is mirrors and chandeliers. Hosts rotate every fifteen minutes with first-time guests; bottles arrive with sparklers; a champagne call makes the whole floor stop, clap and chant a host's name. The ranking board by the door is updated nightly.

lore.when: place: sj_hostclub; period: night; weekend: yes
lore.content: Weekends the room is full by ten: friends on a night out, women celebrating promotions, and one table where a birthday has become a wall of bottles and balloons.
A birthday event for a host: his table becomes a wall of bottles, balloons and gifts, the staff stay late counting, and whoever he picks to stand beside him is the club's gossip for a week.

lore.when: place: sj_hostclub; present: Reiko; present: Shōta; weekday: sat; period: night
lore.content: Reiko Tachibana, in her navy suit, sits with Kaname in the corner booth farthest from the door: her monthly Saturday booking, which nobody mentions. The staff seat her without a word. She talks, he listens, and she leaves well before closing.
Kaname goes to the post office every morning after closing and sends half of what he earned to his mother in Niigata. It is why he keeps so little and why he never takes a day off.
They say Kaname hasn't lost the number-one spot at Club Eternal in two years, and nobody has seen him laugh with a customer the way he laughs when his sister waits up for him.
A host who lets a customer's tab run too high gets a "friendly" introduction to a lender, and that's where the old men who own the buildings come in.
The first customers are managers with clients, brought up in the lift by a hostess who greets them by name. The mama stands at the door and decides which sofa each one deserves.
Low light, ice in glasses, a pianist in the corner some nights. The bill is set by time and seat; the hostesses pour and talk; a bottle with a name tag signals someone who comes often.

lore.when: place: sj_hostess; season: winter; period: evening or night
lore.content: Year-end parties: whole company departments book the largest sofa, bosses sing off-key, and the mama makes sure everyone gets home.
A framed group photo by the lift shows Velvet years ago, the head hostess in a red dress at its center. She now keeps a bar in Golden Gai, and the staff still straighten the frame when they pass.
They say the mama at Lounge Velvet has turned away a big spender for treating a hostess badly, and the room still talks about it.
People say a hostess here pays for her brother's tuition and tells everyone it's for a shop of her own.
At dusk the grills are lit and smoke hangs under the tracks like fog. The alley fills with office workers loosening their ties and the first skewers hit the counters.
Rain drums on the corrugated roofs. People pack the counters for shelter, the smoke hangs low, and every trainload overhead sounds closer than usual.
Half the alley is still prepping: cooks threading skewers, an old woman scrubbing a grill, a few early customers and the trains every two minutes.
Everyone eats with a coat on, hands wrapped around cups of hot sake; the steam of motsu stew fogs the alley's narrow windows.

lore.when: place: sj_omoide; present: Kyōko; period: afternoon or evening
lore.content: Kyōko Shirai is here off duty, in a plain cardigan and no lipstick, turning her empty cigarette holder at a counter by the tracks. The cook calls her Shirai-san; nobody says Mama here. For once someone else pours her beer.
They say the sauce at the third counter was started in 1950 and has never been emptied, only topped up.
Old-timers say the 1999 fire took half the alley in a night, and that it was rebuilt down to the crooked beams.
Six stools, a counter, bottles with names in marker. A stranger sitting next to a regular is a stranger for exactly one drink; after that, whoever the stranger is, the conversation takes them in.
After midnight the alley is shoulder to shoulder, doors propped open, people crossing from bar to bar. At four Mama sets out a bowl of pickles for whoever is left.

lore.when: place: sj_goldengai; present: Reiko; present: Kyōko; weekday: fri; period: night
lore.content: Reiko Tachibana comes every Friday night. When she's here, the karaoke book is hers from eleven, and she sings until closing. Mama never comments.
Doors are propped open, fans whir, and the alley's air smells of beer and mosquito coils.

lore.when: place: sj_goldengai; present: Airi; present: Kyōko; weekday: mon; period: night
lore.content: Airi Mizusawa has the corner stool, sunglasses on and a laugh that carries to the alley. Mama pours her amber whisky and never asks about her work, which is why she comes.

lore.when: place: sj_goldengai; present: Kyōko; present: Sayuri; weekday: sun; period: night
lore.content: On the last Sunday of the season Kotori opens for old friends only. Sayuri Mizuno comes up from Yokohama, the shutters come halfway down, and she and Kyōko trade stories of Velvet until the pickles come out.
They say Mama was the head hostess at Lounge Velvet in its great years, and she won't talk about her Velvet days.
People tell Mama things because she never repeats them, which is why the alley's secrets stay in the alley.
Early in the evening it's quiet: neighbors from the building, a couple on a first date, the bartender slicing lemons and testing the music.
After midnight the stairs fill with friends from other bars. The night goes on in clusters of conversation until the first train.

lore.when: place: sj_nichome; weekend: yes; period: night
lore.content: Saturday night is standing room: someone has brought a cake for someone's birthday and the whole bar is singing, badly.
Rainbow flags hang from the stair railing and the upstairs windows. On the night of the parade Ni-chōme's streets become a party, with music in every doorway and doors propped open.
They say half the couples in the building met on that stair.
People say Lilac's oldest board game has been missing the same piece for ten years and nobody will confess.
The air is cold and clear: the whole bay shows, every district's cluster of towers, and Mt. Fuji with its cap of snow far to the west. Guides say a day like this comes a few times a winter.
At dusk the city lights come on in sections: Tokyo Tower in orange to the south-east, Skytree to the east, and a river of headlights on every avenue. Couples crowd the south windows.
The deck is half empty; the city is a gray carpet under low cloud, and the guides apologize for the view.
From the south windows the pale pink of cherry trees in Shinjuku Gyoen shows as a soft cloud among the rooftops.

lore.when: place: sj_tocho; present: Mei; period: evening
lore.content: Mei Wang, a tablet under her arm, stands alone at the west windows and talks quietly to herself in Mandarin. She comes up some Wednesday evenings to think, and the guides know her face and leave her be.
They say Mt. Fuji shows from the deck only on cold clear mornings, and almost never in summer.
The guides say a couple gets engaged on the deck about once a week, and they've stopped counting.

The cherry trees are in bloom and the gate has a queue. Sheets cover the lawns; no alcohol is allowed in the garden, so people bring tea, sweets and sandwiches. The garden is open every day in cherry season.
Maples in the Japanese garden turn red and a chrysanthemum show fills one corner of the lawn. The garden is gold at four in the afternoon.
The greenhouse is the warmest place in the district; the garden closes early, around half past four, and the light is low and gold.
Cicadas scream from the plane trees. Shade is everything. In the middle of summer the garden stays open until seven, and people bring cold barley tea.
The gardeners can say which cherry tree will bloom first. They're never wrong, and they never say.

After the last train the lobby fills with salarymen who missed it, in rumpled suits, paying at the machine and choosing a capsule. The clerk hands each a locker key, pajamas and a towel without comment.
Early in the evening only travelers are here; the clerk explains the rules (shoes in the locker, quiet after midnight, no phones in the corridor) in three languages.
Friday night the capsules are gone by eleven; Saturday it's tourists and couples, and the clerk puts out an extra stack of towels.
They say the capsules by the vent are the quietest, and the clerks save them for whoever looks like they've had the worst day.

Shimokitazawa, "Shimokita", is a Setagaya neighborhood of narrow lanes behind a station where two small lines cross: vintage shops, record stores, curry counters, small theaters and about twenty live houses, mostly in basements. Cars barely fit, so people walk. Shops open around noon and close by 20:00 or 21:00; many take only cash.

Kōenji, in Suginami ward, is Shimokita's scruffier cousin: punk bands, cheap secondhand clothes, tiny bars and old wooden apartments around a station and a web of covered shopping arcades (Pal, Look and Junjō). Rents are low, nobody dresses up, and the shopkeepers have known each other for decades.

Kōenji's Awa Odori, begun by the arcade's shopkeepers in 1957, runs two days: well over a hundred troupes ("ren") in happi coats dance through the streets to drums, flutes and gongs, chanting "yattosā". Visitors watch; dancers belong to a troupe, usually through a shopkeeper. Tanabata is small: the shopkeepers hang paper strips in early summer.

A sentō is a public bathhouse. Shoes go in a locker; the men's and women's sides are separate and nobody is asked which door they take (a family bath is by appointment). Pay at the raised seat, wash on a stool first, keep the small towel out of the water, finish with milk. Many Tokyo sentō allow tattoos.

Young people here live in share houses (a private room, shared kitchen and bath, a chore rota on the wall) or in apaato, old two-story wooden buildings with tatami, thin walls, a tiny kitchen and often no bath, so the sentō is part of the week. Neighbors know each other's schedules by sound and trade vegetables over the stair rail.

A live house is a small, usually underground music venue with three to five acts a night; the ticket includes a drink ticket and fans queue by ticket number. Small bands must often sell a quota of tickets to friends themselves, so a gig is also a favor asked of everyone they know, and demos are sold at the back.
Ichibangai is Shimokita's busiest run of secondhand clothes and used-book shops, low buildings with hand-painted signs. Haggling is not done; "sale rack" means a rack, and everything else has a tag.

Second Bloom is a vintage clothing shop up a short stair in Shimokitazawa, racks sorted by decade, a record player behind the till. The owner, in her fifties, sits on a stool and says little. Nanami Sera works here.
Vintage here means real decades: 70s coats, 80s jackets, 90s denim. Shops steam and price everything by hand. Haggling is not done; the owner sets the price once.

Basement Moon is a basement live house in Shimokitazawa: a hundred people, black walls covered in stickers, one drink ticket with every ticket. Ren Kujō books the bands and works the door; Paper Lanterns often play the weekend gig here.

Theater Komorebi is a sixty-seat fringe theater up an outside stair in Shimokitazawa, above a small bar. Komorebi is the sun through leaves; here it is the skylight that drops a patch of light on the stage every afternoon. Thursday nights are comedy.

Curry Hanabi is a soup-curry shop in Shimokitazawa: thin spiced soup, a chicken leg, big roasted vegetables, rice on the side. Spice is a number from one to ten and the cook never recommends above five. Shimokita is known as a curry town and the line at lunch proves it.

A kissaten is an old-style coffee house: dim, quiet, siphon or hand-drip coffee, set meals, and no one hurries a guest from one cup. Kissa Shirakaba, "white birch", is a 1970s one in Shimokitazawa, run by a master in a bow tie. A morning set is served until eleven.

Matsu-no-yu, "pine bath", is an old public bathhouse in Kōenji run by one family: a temple-style roof, a chimney, a pine on the curtain and a mural of Mt. Fuji repainted every few years. It opens in the afternoon, closes at midnight, shuts one weekday, and doesn't mind tattoos.

The attendant sits on a raised seat at the door that overlooks both changing rooms: takes payment, sells towels, hands out locker keys, watches the bath's temperature, and gives a look to anyone who forgets to rinse.

The arcade south of Kōenji station is a covered shopping street of secondhand clothes, record shops, a fishmonger, a butcher with croquettes, izakaya and tiny restaurants. Its shopkeepers began the Awa Odori in 1957 and still run it.

Moonlight Mart Kōenji is a 24-hour convenience store by the station. Mio Hayasaka works night shifts. A konbini sells meals, coffee, hot snacks, umbrellas and train tickets, takes bill payments and parcels, and has an ATM. Clerks greet each customer and ask if the food should be warmed; no one tips.

Studio Tsubame is a small anime studio in a converted house on the Kōenji side; tsubame is the swallow, and one nests over the door every spring. Haru Aoki animates here. Freelancers are paid by the drawing, staff on the ladder by the hour; deadlines are fierce and people stay because they love it.
Making anime: key animators draw the important poses, in-betweeners draw the frames between them, and a director decides what stays. Beginners earn little and learn by being corrected.
The lanes are packed with students, couples and shoppers; clothes racks spill onto the pavement and bar touts hand out flyers for tonight's gigs.
lore.when: place: ws_shimokita; weekend: yes; period: afternoon or evening

lore.content: Different bands leak from different basements, drums from one stairwell, a guitar from the next; before midnight the lanes stream toward the station for the last train.
lore.when: place: ws_shimokita; period: night; weekend: no

lore.content: Wool coats and leather jackets come out on the racks; the lanes smell of roasted chestnuts and curry.
A queue forms at the fitting curtain; shoppers pass pieces between friends and hold them to the light.
Coats take over the racks; a small heater by the till glows and the window shows wool, fake fur and scarves.
The last hour before closing: the owner puts a record on, and Nanami hums along while she folds, a half-tone sharp on purpose.
lore.when: place: ws_vintage; period: evening; present: Nanami

lore.content: Sound check leaks up the stairs; a line forms at the street door in ticket-number order, fans in band tees with a flyer in one hand.
The room is hot and packed; hands go up; after the last song the lights come on and everyone files out for the last train while the band stands at the merch table.
lore.when: place: ws_livehouse; event: livehouse_gig; period: night

lore.content: A thin crowd of ten, a bartender and a band that plays as if the room were full; this is where bands really learn.
lore.when: place: ws_livehouse; weekend: no; period: night

lore.content: Ren stamps hands at the door with a lazy flick, knows half the queue by name, and checks the setlist against the clock without looking worried.
lore.when: place: ws_livehouse; period: evening or night; present: Ren

lore.content: Paper Lanterns take the stage: Nanami at the mic in her leather jacket, Kaito behind the kit with his cap turned backwards, Ren low on the bass. The first song is loud and nobody looks at anyone; by the second song they do.
lore.when: place: ws_livehouse; event: livehouse_gig; period: night; present: Ren; present: Nanami; present: Kaito

lore.content: Rehearsal: actors in tracksuits repeat a single scene, the stage manager shouts "from the top", and the light from the skylight crosses the boards.
A line forms on the outside stair; tickets are sold from a card table and reserved by name; the audience goes in with a drink from the bar.
No air conditioning: the audience is handed paper fans and the actors perform through the heat; the skylight is propped open.
Rain on the roof becomes part of the play; the stair is slick and the audience steams as it goes in.
The lunch line runs down the stairs; shop clerks in aprons eat in twenty minutes and go back. The server shouts spice levels across the counter.
lore.when: place: ws_curry; period: afternoon; weekend: no

lore.content: Windows fog white; people stamp in from the cold and order a five to warm up; the soup steams for the whole of the meal.
Regulars order the hottest level and sweat it out; fans turn, and a pitcher of cold barley tea is refilled without being asked.
A slower hour: actors from Theater Komorebi eat before curtain and couples split one big bowl.
Toast and coffee scent; old men read newspapers; the master wipes siphon flasks. A morning set arrives with a clack of china.
Nearly empty: a student writes in a booth, a radio plays low, sun comes through the yellow lace.
A small stove ticks by the counter; the windows fog and coats stay on until the second cup.
Iced coffee and cream soda in tall glasses; an old fan turns in the corner and the lace curtains move.
Seo-yeon sets each cup down with both hands, a film camera swinging on its strap, and steers readers to the second table, where the light is best. She writes in a small notebook between orders.
Ren reads at the second table with his notebook beside the cup; Seo-yeon refills his water more often than he needs and pretends not to look at the notebook.
lore.when: place: ws_kissaten; present: Seo-yeon; present: Ren

lore.content: On her break Seo-yeon props her phone against the sugar jar and speaks fast, soft Korean to her mother's face on the screen. When the talk turns to her studies she says "economics" in careful Japanese and angles the screen away; her notebook, full of a novel set in this very shop, stays closed until the call ends.
lore.when: place: ws_kissaten; present: Seo-yeon; feels: Seo-yeon friend; season: not winter

lore.content: Natsuki and Haru share the back booth and pass sketchbooks across the table, trading one-word verdicts ("flat", "nice hands", "stolen"); Natsuki's headphones hang round her neck and Haru's ink-stained fingers turn the page.
lore.when: place: ws_kissaten; weekday: sun; period: afternoon; present: Natsuki; present: Haru

lore.content: The after-work rush: men in suits become wet-haired, washing stools clack, the attendant runs towels and a television plays the news over the baths.
The last hour before closing: the water goes still, the attendant mops, a few late bathers float and talk in low voices under the lit mural.
Steam rolls out of the door and fogs the street; around midwinter yuzu citrus float in the bath and the whole room smells of it.
Iris leaves float in the bath for Golden Week, a custom said to keep illness away; they smell sharp and green.
The cold plunge is the popular tub; people come at opening, sweat, rinse and walk home in the evening heat with a bottle of milk.
Chloe sits in the lobby with a milk and pink cheeks, chatting with the grandmothers in half-Japanese and half-Manchester, and will gladly explain the rules to any newcomer.
lore.when: place: ws_sento; period: evening or night; present: Chloe

lore.content: Drums, flutes and gongs from troupes practicing in corners of the arcade, sandals slapping the ground in sixteen-bar loops, and the call of "yattosā"; shopkeepers watch from their doorways with their arms folded.
A few bamboo branches hung with colored paper strips stand outside shops; the shopkeepers keep pens in a jar and the strips flutter in the warm air.

Awa Odori: troupes pour through the arcade and the streets around it in happi coats, to drums, flutes and gongs; the pavements are packed with people watching, and the whole district smells of food stalls and sweat.
Most shutters are down and the izakaya lanterns are lit; the arcade echoes with late drinkers and bicycles.
The arcade is a refuge: rain rattles the awning, the crowd squeezes under it and umbrellas drip in the doorways.
Past midnight: drunk groups, taxi drivers on break and delivery riders; the clerk mops, restocks bread, and the fridges hum.
Salarymen grab rice-balls and coffee; a line forms at the coffee machine; the fresh lunch boxes arrive off a truck.
The oden pot steams by the register; the clerk lifts the lid for each order and the glass doors mist over.
The ice-cream freezer is the busiest corner; people stand in front of the cold drinks until the clerk coughs.
Mio hums while she mops and greets even the drunkest salaryman as if he were a guest; the shelf labels are straighter on her shifts.
lore.when: place: ws_konbini; period: latenight; present: Mio

lore.content: Linh, in a cardigan over her care-worker scrubs after a night shift, buys a rice-ball and a milk tea and practices a polite phrase on the clerk, her jade bracelet clicking on the counter.
lore.when: place: ws_konbini; period: firsttrain or rush; present: Linh

lore.content: While Mio restocks the morning bread, Linh stands beside her with her breakfast and the two talk in low, tired voices about their shifts.
lore.when: place: ws_konbini; period: firsttrain; weekday: mon or thu; present: Linh; present: Mio

lore.content: Every lamp burns; the rice cooker clicks; pencils scratch; someone sleeps under a desk and nobody steps over them quietly.
A quiet scratching of pencils, a kettle in the kitchen and a radio kept low; nobody speaks unless they must.
The swallows have returned; one repairs its nest over the door and the staff look out at it between drawings.
Fans run, the back room has no air conditioning, and drawings are held down with mugs against the draft.
Haru works hunched over a key drawing, silver ear cuffs catching the lamp, ink on their fingers; they answer in single words without looking up.
Camille, the exchange-student intern, sits cross-legged on the floor with charcoal on her cheek, in-betweening in halting Japanese and answering any question with a philosophy of drawing.
Haru corrects Camille's in-betweens without a word, a pencil line over hers; she stares at the correction for a long time before she redraws it.
lore.when: place: ws_studio; present: Camille; present: Haru

lore.content: Linh climbs the iron stairs in her scrubs, shoes in one hand so as not to wake the building, and falls asleep sitting up over her care-exam notes.
lore.when: zone: hz_apaato; present: Linh; period: firsttrain or rush

lore.content: Behind a second-floor door with a hand-lettered circle nameplate, Kanon draws adult doujinshi until dawn: pens, screen-tone sheets, and game soundtracks leaking through the thin walls. She answers the door in track pants with a pen behind her ear, and lights up if anyone mentions her work.

Pinned to the fridge under a magnet, among the chore and bath rotas, a small ink drawing of Mio mid-laugh over a bowl of rice: unsigned, new since yesterday. Mio thinks Chloe draws them and thanks her at breakfast; Chloe plays along; Haru eats cereal with their hood up and watches the door.
They say Studio Tsubame is animating a series for next season and nobody is allowed to say which.
Neighbors say the lights in the old house haven't gone out before two in the morning since spring.
They say the best record shop in the lanes keeps its rarest records in the apartment upstairs and only shows them after your third visit.
Shopkeepers grumble that the lanes are on every tourist map now and the good racks go to whoever opens first.
Second Bloom's owner is said to keep a 1970s leather jacket in the back that she has refused to sell for years.
They say half the shop's coats came out of a retired theater costume designer's wardrobe.
Word on the lanes is a label scout stood at the back of Basement Moon last Friday, asking about the singer of Paper Lanterns.
lore.when: region: westside; season: summer or autumn; chance: 0.25

lore.content: They say the basement floods in a heavy rain, and the owner keeps a pump behind the stage and a bucket brigade on speed dial.
They say Komorebi's director turned down a TV drama to stay on a sixty-seat stage.
People say a famous comedian started on the Thursday stage before anyone knew his name.
They say the Hanabi cook toasts the spices himself at four in the morning and won't tell his own cousin the blend.
Locals claim the level-ten bowl has been finished exactly once, by a visiting rugby team's prop forward, who had to be helped to the door.
They say the master was a jazz pianist before he took the shop over, and the old upright in the back still works.
Regulars swear the wall clock has been eight minutes fast since 1979 and set their lunch by it.
Locals say the owner has turned down a condo developer three times and the fourth offer is bigger.
An old bather swears the Fuji painter, one of the last in Tokyo, did the mural in a single night.
They say the bathhouse's boiler is older than the owner and has its own name.
They say a troupe of old shopkeepers has danced every year since the first Awa Odori and one of them is ninety.
Neighbors have complained for years about drumming in the park at midnight in July, and nobody has ever stopped it.
The night clerks say a man comes at 3:12 every night for the same canned coffee and never says a word.
They say the vending machine out front has swapped its hot and cold coffee, and the clerks bet on which will come out.

Akihabara, "Akiba", began as a postwar market for radio parts and became the district of electronics, then games, anime and idols. Its main street, Electric Town, is bright and crowded all day; shops close around eight, arcades and cafés later. Almost everyone here is a fan of something and talks about it with total sincerity.

A small-theater idol show is songs and dances a few steps from the audience. Fans pick an "oshi" (a favorite member), wave glow sticks and shout rehearsed chants. After the show a "cheki" (an instant photo, about ¥1,000) buys ten seconds of chat and a pose; no touching, no personal questions. Groups often forbid members to date.

In a maid café, staff in maid uniforms play characters: they greet customers as "master" or "princess" ("welcome home"), draw pictures on omurice in ketchup and cast a "moe moe" spell over the food. It's theater, not flirting: customers pay a table charge, take instant photos, and never touch the staff or ask personal questions.

Kanda Myōjin, founded in 730, is the old guardian shrine of Edo's merchants: it honors Daikokuten and Ebisu, gods of fortune and trade, and Taira no Masakado, once feared and now revered. Engineers buy circuit-board charms for working computers; fans hang hand-drawn anime ema (wish plaques). The grounds never close; the charm office shuts at five.

Jinbōchō is a short walk from Akiba and holds one of the densest runs of used bookshops anywhere, with old curry houses and coffee shops among them. Shops open around ten or eleven, close in the early evening, and many close on Sundays and holidays. The used-book festival lines Yasukuni-dōri with carts for ten days each autumn.

A game center stacks floors by taste: prizes low, rhythm and fighting games higher, photo booths ("purikura") on their own floor, medal games at the top. Plays cost ¥100 to ¥300 and cash is common. Staff nudge a prize closer if asked. Top rhythm-game players wait their turn in silence, and a hush falls when someone plays well.

Café Mille-Feuille is a maid café up a narrow staircase in Akiba, all pink and cream, with a stage the size of a table. The maids stay in character from the stairs to the till; only in the kitchen do they relax. The omurice is better than a gimmick café needs.

Pixel Castle is a seven-floor game center in Akiba. Prize machines fill the first floors, rhythm cabinets the fourth, photo booths the fifth, medal games the top. Retirees and gamers wait outside at opening.

Tempo Tower is the rhythm game on the fourth floor: six buttons, pounding songs, and a leaderboard of hyphenated aliases. The top spot has belonged to "NATSU-P" for months, a name everyone knows and nobody has put a face to.

Stage Starlight is a small idol theater in a basement in Akiba, with shows every evening and a bigger one on Saturday. Its house group, Hanabira Signal, has five members and a loyal small following. The rules are strict: no dating, no phones on stage, cheki only at the table.

Mochi Byte Games is a nine-person indie studio in Akiba whose cozy puzzle game "Mochi Hop" paid for the office. The team is now building a second game and deciding how big to dream. Natsuki Fujii works there as a programmer.

Comic Cocoon is a manga and internet café in Akiba: thousands of volumes, private booths, a drink bar and showers. It's open all night, and a night pack costs ¥2,500. Many people miss their last train and sleep here, and some people here have nowhere else.

Seiran Prep School is one of the prep-school towers in the Ochanomizu and Surugadai quarter, near several universities and the shops that sell guitars by the street. Its candidates are adults retaking exams (rōnin), changing careers or sitting certificates. Before an exam they pray at Yushima Tenjin shrine nearby.

Hijiri University is a private university by the Ochanomizu bridges, with brick lecture halls, a Japanese language center in an old annex and an art faculty whose studios stay lit late. Its students are adults: third and fourth years starting their job hunt, and exchange students living in the international dorm. In autumn the campus festival fills the lawns with stalls and bands.

On car-free Sunday the main street is shut to cars in the afternoon. People walk down the middle, cosplayers pose for photos, and signs forbid bicycles, flyers and street performances. It is cancelled at short notice in rain, and ends an hour earlier in autumn and winter.
Umbrellas jam the pavements, the car-free Sunday is called off, and the arcades fill. The maids on the corners hold their menu boards under clear umbrellas.
The parts stalls under the tracks are shuttered by now. The signs, the claw-machine glow and the touts keep the street lit, and the crowd drifts to arcades, ramen counters and the last cafés.

Kanon Shiraishi, a grown woman in a hoodie and track pants, walks the used-doujinshi shops with her hood up and stops at the boxes of adult games in the windows. She avoids eye contact and lights up if someone names a game she loves.
A line of fans waits on the stairs. A table is sixty minutes and an order; a maid announces the time with a smile, and nobody argues.
lore.when: place: ak_maid; period: afternoon; weekend: yes

lore.content: The maids never break character where customers can see them, never touch customers, and never share private details. A wrong guess about "who she really is" ends the conversation, politely.
The seasonal menu has cherry-blossom omurice with a pink sauce, and a maid in a petal-print apron draws a tree on it.
By closing the café is half empty; the maids tidy, and a regular finishes the last spell of the day in a whisper.
Weekend floors are packed with groups; the rhythm cabinets have a quiet queue, the prize machines a noisy one, and staff walk around with a handheld counter for the line.
Salarymen in loosened ties play alone before their last train, and the top floor is nearly silent apart from the medal machines.
Retirees take the medal floor at opening and gamers wait at the new cabinets; staff polish the glass and run the first test plays.

On Friday nights Natsuki Fujii and Hannah Becker take two rhythm cabinets side by side and trade high scores in the tight silence of rivals; Hannah's dry puns land half a second late and Natsuki answers with a flawless chart. Regulars leave them a cabinet's width of space.
lore.when: place: ak_arcade; present: Natsuki; present: Hannah; weekday: fri; period: night

lore.content: The Saturday show packs the basement. Glow sticks move together, the chants are loud and exact, and the group's smiles never flicker.
Natsuki Fujii stands in the back row every Saturday, silent, never joining the chants, and leaves before the cheki line forms.
lore.when: place: ak_idol; present: Natsuki; weekday: sat

lore.content: Hina Asano, lilac twin tails and a bright smile on stage, switches off the moment the curtain closes. At the cheki table she gives ten seconds of full warmth and counts every one.

Hina has started counting the shows left in the season under her breath, and during the last song her eyes drift to the exit sign. She hasn't told the theater she is thinking of graduating, and she would tell {{user}} before anyone else.
lore.when: place: ak_idol; present: Hina; feels: Hina good

lore.content: Before the doors open the stage belongs to the trainers: counts of eight, a song on loop, members repeating a turn until their knees hurt.
Members call it "the rules": no dating, no social media of their own, no being seen off duty with a fan. Some accept it as the price of the stage; some count the days.
Crunch looks gentle here: a desk lamp, a developer eating noodles over a keyboard, a producer ordering pizza with an apology. The deadline is real, and nobody says it aloud.
The morning standup is ten minutes of people reading their own tasks, then a long silence while a bug is blamed on a cat.
lore.when: place: ak_gamedev; period: midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: A game fair is near; the demo kiosk is tuned for a crowd, and everyone has the same dream of a long line.

Hannah Becker works the localization desk by the window, typing without looking and muttering German when a line of dialogue won't translate. Her Japanese puns land half a second late, and the team has learned to wait for them.
Hannah and her colleague Natsuki trade rhythm-game scores on sticky notes pinned beside the build monitor; the wall of scores has grown into a small rivalry anyone can read.
lore.when: place: ak_gamedev; present: Hannah; period: afternoon

lore.content: Rina Tachibana sits across the demo kiosk from Natsuki with two phones face-up and a deck open, talking terms for the second game. The talks have stalled over who owns what; Natsuki answers in half-sentences and watches the producer's face.
lore.when: place: ak_gamedev; present: Rina; present: Natsuki; period: afternoon; weekend: no

lore.content: With the last trains gone, booths fill with salarymen in shirtsleeves and young workers on a budget; the clerk hands out thin blankets, and a hundred people sleep without a sound.
Curtains open one by one as the first train nears; people queue for the shower in rumpled clothes, brushing their teeth in silence before they rejoin the day.
Freelancers and remote workers take the booths as offices, laptops on the little desks; the clerk knows who needs the outlet by the window.

Hannah Becker takes the corner booth in a hood and a headset. A friend who leans in recognizes her deadpan voice coming from a cartoon owl in a mortarboard on her screen: a streamer who teaches Japanese to thousands of foreigners. Hannah freezes, then asks {{user}} very quietly to keep it from Mochi Byte.
lore.when: place: ak_mangacafe; present: Hannah; feels: Hannah friend

lore.content: Kanon Shiraishi, a grown woman in a hoodie and track pants, hides in a corner booth with a sketchbook and a night pack to draw away from her cramped flat. She speaks to nobody unless asked about her drawings, then talks too fast.

At Setsubun, invited guests throw lucky beans from a raised platform and a crowd packs the courtyard, hands up. Afterwards everyone eats as many beans as their age. Noisy, cheerful, and careful of the old.
The courtyard is empty and still; the grounds are open but the charm office is shuttered, and a lone salaryman bows at the gate on his way to the station.
Office workers stop at the gate on the way to work, drop a coin, bow once and hurry on; the priests sweep the courtyard before the charm office opens.
lore.when: place: ak_myojin; period: rush or midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: Prayer here follows the shrine's order: a bow at the gate, two bows, two claps and one bow at the hall, and a wish for work, a deal, a shipping date or a server that stays up.
Many bookshops are closed on Sundays and holidays; the streets are quiet, shutters down, only the curry houses and a few coffee shops open. Saturday is the real market day.
The used-book festival lines the main avenue with carts for ten days: bargain tables, readers shoulder to shoulder, people carrying stacks home in bags that are already tearing.
The lunch line at the old curry house curls round the corner; people in suits eat in ten minutes and walk back to their desks reading a paperback.
Shop owners drag the carts under the awnings and wrap books in plastic; the street smells of wet paper.
Exam season: the study room is full by nine, heaters tick, instant noodles steam on every desk, and nobody speaks above a whisper. Charm bags hang from pencil cases.
Evening classes end around ten; candidates drift out in twos and threes and talk in low voices on the bridge over the Kanda River.
Weekends mean practice exams: a long silent hall, rustling paper and a clock that everyone watches.
Food stalls line the lawns, run by clubs and by exchange students cooking dishes from home; a stage hosts bands and dance circles, and the lecture halls turn into cafés and haunted houses.
The lecture halls fill, and the language center's stairwell echoes with students practicing greetings in four languages.
lore.when: place: ak_university; period: midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: Club rooms light up one by one: cameras and film cans, shin guards and a ball, drawing boards. The long block hums until the library's lights are the only ones left.
lore.when: place: ak_university; period: evening; weekend: no

lore.content: Exam season: the library's reading room is full by nine, the club rooms are dark, and students carry thermoses and photocopied notes everywhere.
Seo-yeon Park reads by the library's east window with her beret on the desk and a film camera in her lap, answering questions in careful, formal Japanese and photographing the light on the page.
At dusk Seo-yeon walks the river bank behind campus photographing bridges, and she talks more easily outdoors than in a hall.
lore.when: place: ak_university; present: Seo-yeon; period: evening

lore.content: Camille Laurent sits cross-legged on the steps with a sketchbook, rolling a cigarette she'll smoke only in the smoking area, and turns any small talk into a philosophical argument.
Camille is more often in the art annex or the smoking area than in a lecture seat, and the language-center teachers have stopped being surprised.
lore.when: place: ak_university; present: Camille; period: midmorning

lore.content: Lucas Oliveira crosses the quad in a football shirt, greeting every table in Portuguese-flavored Japanese; he's headed for the engineering labs or the pitch, and flirts with everyone equally.
Lucas plays futsal on the sports ground under the floodlights, shouting instructions in Portuguese and conceding every argument with a grin.
lore.when: place: ak_university; present: Lucas; period: evening

lore.content: Mio Hayasaka, an art-faculty student from Sendai in paint-stained overalls, sketches in the art annex between night shifts and dozes in the back row of the lecture hall with a pencil still in her hand.

Mio's autumn exams are close and she is behind in two courses: she studies in the library with her sketchbook shut and changes the subject when anyone asks about grades. Her parents in Sendai don't know, and she would tell a friend first.
lore.when: place: ak_university; present: Mio; season: autumn; feels: Mio friend

lore.content: After ten the kitchen fills with students cooking dishes from home, the curfew is a rumor, and the warden pretends to sleep.
They say a stall under the tracks has a prototype console nobody ever bought, sitting in a box behind the cables.
The ward keeps tightening the rules on touts, so the maids now stand with a sign instead of walking up to people.
They say the little stage at Mille-Feuille was built from the counter of the coffee shop that used to be there.
They say someone on the fourth floor once beat the top Tempo Tower score on a bad cabinet with one broken button, and walked out without a word.
Some fans say a man has been waiting at the stage door after the Saturday show, and the staff walk the members to the station now.
Someone says a startup founder keeps coming by Mochi Byte, and the second game might get funded or might get swallowed.
They say Comic Cocoon sells out its flat booths every Sunday night, when people dread Monday.
People say a plaque with a plain wish, "let us ship on time", hangs among the anime ema, and a whole studio signed it.
A shop owner swears people keep finding old letters in the used books, and that some were never sent.
A star lecturer at Seiran is said to know every candidate's name, and to have never once been late.
They say the library's top floor stays open after the rest of campus shuts, and the night guard lets in anyone who looks truly desperate before an exam.

Shitamachi, the "low city" along the Sumida, is old Tokyo of merchants and craftspeople: family shops that close at six, neighbors who know each other's business, blunt quick speech, and pride in festivals. Asakusa, Ueno and Yanaka are its heart.

Sensō-ji, Tokyo's oldest temple, is dedicated to Kannon; the story says two fishermen netted her statue from the Sumida in 628. The red Thunder Gate with its giant lantern leads down Nakamise, the lane of snack and souvenir stalls, to the main hall. The grounds never close.

At Sensō-ji, people shake a metal box until a numbered stick falls out and take the matching slip from its drawer. Good luck is kept; bad luck (kyō) is tied to the rack and left behind, with no shame, and the temple is known for handing out plenty of it. Incense smoke is wafted over whatever ails a person. At a temple, prayer is quiet; clapping is for shrines.

Ueno Park holds the museums, the zoo, a shrine, and Shinobazu Pond with its lotuses. At hanami the newest employee lays a blue sheet at dawn to hold a spot; by evening it is food, drink and lanterns, and everyone carries their trash home.

Ameyoko is the loud market street along the railway tracks between Ueno and Okachimachi, born from the black market after the war: fish, dried goods, spices, sneakers, shouted prices, mostly cash. It's at its craziest in the last days of December.

Yanaka escaped both the 1923 earthquake and the wartime fires, so its wooden houses, temples and a big cemetery survive. Its little shopping street, Yanaka Ginza, is full of croquettes and cat figures, and real cats sit on the walls. Visitors are asked to keep their voices down.

Rickshaw pullers wait by the Thunder Gate in happi coats and split-toe shoes. They pull two passengers around the lanes, tell stories as they run, and charge by the half hour. A good puller never lets the ride shake.

At the main hall of Sensō-ji, people toss a coin into the offering box, bow, pray quietly with palms together and bow again; there is no clapping at a temple. Many first wash their hands at the fountain and stop at the incense burner on the way up.

The Sumida riverside walk runs along both banks, lined with cherry trees; across the water stands the Skytree, 634 meters tall. Water buses glide down to the bay. The river's fireworks go back to 1733.

Izakaya Daruma is an open-front stew shop on a lantern-lit lane near Sensō-ji, open from noon. It has no sign, only a daruma doll in the window, and the best stew in Asakusa, slow-simmered, with beer. An evening costs about ¥3,500.
Ueno Hall of Art is a quiet museum in Ueno Park with a collection of Japanese paintings and prints and a new special exhibition each season. It is closed on Mondays; the café is on the ground floor.

Ramen Kamejirō is a twelve-seat shop in Asakusa run by Genzō Kamei for forty years; its pork-bone broth has never gone cold. His daughter Ayaka works with him. Customers buy a ticket at the machine by the door.
Ramen in Tokyo: people slurp loudly (it's polite), eat fast, don't linger when there's a line, and order extra noodles ("kaedama") instead of a second bowl.

Tsukimi Inari is a small fox shrine in Yanaka run by the Kanzaki family: a short row of red gates, stone foxes in red bibs, a charm window. Neighbors leave fried tofu for the foxes. The name means "moon-viewing", after a legend of foxes dancing in the moonlight.
At Tsukimi Inari, people bow at the gate, then bow twice, clap twice and bow once more before the small hall, and leave a plate of fried tofu for the foxes. Sometimes a cat gets there first.
Company outings follow flags down Nakamise, retirees on a club trip pose at the gate, exchange students queue at the omikuji stand, and stall keepers push free samples of rice crackers into hands.
lore.when: place: ot_sensoji; period: midmorning or afternoon

lore.content: The stalls have pulled down their shutters, painted with scenes of old Asakusa. The hall, pagoda and gates are lit gold, and the lane is empty except for locals and the echo of footsteps.
lore.when: place: ot_sensoji; period: evening or night

lore.content: The grounds are open and nearly empty: a monk sweeping, a few old neighbors praying before work. The main hall opens at six.
Umbrellas jam the lane, the incense smoke hangs low and smells stronger, and the rickshaws fold their hoods and wait; the pullers shelter under the gate and trade stories.

For the Sanja Matsuri, portable shrines from the neighboring Asakusa Shrine are carried through the streets by men and women in happi coats; drums, whistles and shouting, and Nakamise packed past walking.
On New Year's Eve, people queue in the cold with soba in their stomachs; at midnight the temple bell rings 108 times and the line surges toward the hall.
lore.when: place: ot_sensoji; festival: omisoka; period: night or latenight

lore.content: An old ramen master in his good coat and a woman in a kimono-style coat stand a little apart in the line, not speaking, as the bell begins.
lore.when: place: ot_sensoji; festival: omisoka; period: night or latenight; present: Genzō; present: Kyōko

lore.content: They say the omikuji box at Sensō-ji hands out more bad fortunes than any other in Tokyo, and that the temple likes it that way.
A rickshaw puller at the gate says he once pulled the same couple on their first date and on their fiftieth anniversary.
The cherry trees along both banks are in flower; petals float on the water and walkers stop to photograph the Skytree through the branches.
The Skytree is lit and reflected in the black water; runners pass, couples sit shoulder to shoulder on the steps, and a water bus slides by with its lights on.
lore.when: place: ot_sumida; period: evening or night

lore.content: On the riverside courts a pickup futsal game is under way: Kaito, cap backwards, runs the wing in a rider jacket tossed on the grass, and Lucas, in a football shirt, calls plays in Portuguese and argues every foul with a grin; there is room for one more on either side.
lore.when: place: ot_sumida; weekday: sun; period: rush or midmorning; present: Kaito; present: Lucas

lore.content: On the fireworks night the riverbanks are packed from the afternoon: yukata, folding stools, food bought on the way. Streets close, and the booms are felt in the chest.
For moon viewing, locals set out dumplings and pampas grass on the stone steps and talk quietly under the bridge lights.
They say the water-bus captains race each other on the last run of the evening and the conductors pretend not to notice.
Old men are already drinking at noon with the TV on a race; the owner pretends not to notice who is on the clock.
The lane fills with tables and cigarette smoke; salarymen loosen their ties and toast each other's bosses.
Plastic sheeting is drawn across the open front and the stew pot fogs the glass; hot sake is poured over the counter.
Genzō Kamei has the corner seat nearest the lane; the owner sets down his beer before he has sat, and neither says a word.
lore.when: place: ot_izakaya; period: night; present: Genzō

lore.content: They say the owner of Daruma reads out the race results from his radio every afternoon, and that nobody orders until the last one is done.
The daruma doll has one eye; they say the owner will paint the other the day the shop turns fifty.
Hundreds of blue tarps cover the ground under the cherry trees; juniors who held spots since dawn guard the corners, while pink lanterns light up as evening comes.
The lotus leaves cover Shinobazu Pond like green plates, and pink flowers open at dawn; a few old men photograph them before the crowds come.
The ginkgos along the avenues turn gold and carpet the paths; the museums fill with people who came to get out of the cool wind.
Performers draw crowds on the plaza and the boats are all out; the park hums until dusk.
Outside hanami, the park is dark and empty past the pond; a few joggers and a figure asleep on a bench. Everyone leaves by eleven.
They say the lotus on Shinobazu Pond blooms a day earlier every year, and the old men with cameras have been keeping score.
They say the best hanami spots go to whoever lays the tarp before five in the morning, and that one company sends its juniors at three.
Couples on a slow weekday and art students have the galleries almost to themselves; the only sound is soft shoes and the guards' coughs.
lore.when: place: ot_museum; period: midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: A queue for the special exhibition runs down the steps; people whisper, audio guides in ears, and nobody stays long at any one painting.
The museum fills with people sheltering; umbrellas drip in a long rack by the door, and even the café is packed.
On Fridays the museum stays open late: a quiet crowd of office workers in lanyards drifts through the galleries, and the café sells out of cake.
lore.when: place: ot_museum; weekday: fri; period: evening

lore.content: A young woman in a camel trench coat and a beret drifts from room to room with a film camera on a strap, photographing the light on the floors rather than the paintings; the guards nod to her as to a regular.
lore.when: place: ot_museum; weekday: sun; period: afternoon; present: Seo-yeon

lore.content: They say the museum café's cake sells out by noon on the day a new exhibition opens, and the guides save themselves a slice before the doors open.
The guards are said to bet on which painting visitors will stand before longest, and the winner is always the small one in the corner.
Prices are shouted: "ten for a thousand yen!" The crowd is shoulder to shoulder, the air smells of grilled seafood and spice, and everything is cash.
lore.when: place: ot_ameyoko; period: midmorning or afternoon

lore.content: Stalls pull their shutters; the standing bars under the railway arches light up, and every train overhead makes the glasses hum.
In the last days of December the street is jammed with people buying crab, roe, sea bream and chestnuts for the New Year's feast; shouting rises to its peak.
The arches keep the rain off; the crowd packs under them, umbrellas folded, and the roar of trains swallows the shouting.
They say Ameyoko got its name from the candy sold here after the war; others swear it's from the American goods that came off the base.
The fishmongers say "ten for a thousand yen" hasn't changed in thirty years; only the size of the fish has.
Shops close at six; the stair fills with people to watch the sunset, an old woman puts out a saucer, and the cats appear on the walls on cue.
Visitors with cameras whisper along the shopping street; signs ask them to keep their voices down for the people who live here.
Cherry trees line the cemetery road and the petals pile up on the old graves; the last shogun is buried here, and people stop at his tomb.
Cicadas scream and wind chimes ring from open doorways; old men fan themselves on stoops and cats sleep in the shade of every wall.

On the quiet Tuesday afternoon two women in their twenties share croquettes on the stairs: Ayaka, still smelling of broth, with a foil packet of chashu scraps for the cats, and Yui in a cardigan, scolding her for feeding pork to the shrine's neighbors; Ayaka does it anyway, and they argue in the same Yanaka accent.
lore.when: place: ot_yanaka; weekday: tue; period: afternoon; present: Ayaka; present: Yui

lore.content: People say the web novelist "Moon Fox" lives somewhere in Yanaka, and every grandmother on the lane has her own theory.
One stray in Yanaka is fed by thirty households and every one of them calls it by a different name.
The lunch line runs down the street; office workers eat in ten minutes and leave without a word.
lore.when: place: ot_ramen; period: afternoon; weekend: no

lore.content: The last customers are regulars; Genzō pours himself a small beer and sometimes talks.
The window is fogged white from the broth; people come in stamping the cold off their feet.
Ayaka runs the floor in her bandana and apron: she calls each order over her shoulder, teases the regulars by name, thumps the ticket machine when it sticks, and keeps one eye on her father's hands.
They say Kamejirō might close this year; the landlord was seen measuring the shop.
lore.when: region: oldtown; season: autumn or winter; chance: 0.2

lore.content: They say the foxes' red bibs are replaced every month by someone no one has ever seen.
A neighbor prays, the priest is away at a ritual, and the charm window is open; the only sounds are the broom and the wind in the pines.
lore.when: place: ot_shrine; period: midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: A single lantern glows at the gate; the fox bibs look nearly black, and a cat sits on the top step like a third fox.
At moon viewing the family sets out dumplings and pampas grass at the haiden; neighbors come to look at the moon through the torii.
On New Year's Eve the shrine stays open all night: a bonfire for last year's charms, warm sweet sake from a pot, and a line of neighbors in coats stretching down the steps.
Neighbors say the fried tofu left for the foxes is always gone by morning, and the cat takes the blame.

Tokyo Station's red-brick Marunouchi building opened in 1914, burned in 1945 and was restored in 2012 with its two domes. Bullet trains leave from the Yaesu side behind it. Marunouchi, the business quarter in front, is towers, lobbies and lanyards, and nearly empty on weekends.

Ginza is named for a silver mint set up there in 1612. It is Tokyo's classic shopping street: department stores, galleries and counters that have sold one thing for a century. On weekend and holiday afternoons Chūō-dōri closes to cars from noon and people walk in the road.

At a Tokyo company a business card is taken with both hands and read before it is pocketed; papers pass through the seals (hanko) of everyone senior; leaving before the boss is awkward. Seniors are senpai, juniors kōhai, and "otsukaresama desu" ("thank you for your hard work") is said to everyone, all day.

A nomikai is a drinking party after work: the first round is beer for everyone, juniors pour for seniors, and no glass sits empty. The bōnenkai, the year-end party, is the big one: in the first days of winter whole sections fill the izakaya "to forget the year", and a second party usually follows.

At Yūrakuchō dozens of tiny izakaya sit in the brick arches under the railway (gādo-shita, "beneath the girders"). Red lanterns, plastic stools in the street, grill smoke pouring out, and an elevated train rumbling over every few minutes. Office workers have drunk here for decades.

The Imperial Palace stands on the grounds of Edo Castle, the shoguns' seat; its stone walls, gates and moat remain. The East Gardens are the free public part; the emperor's residence is not open. The path around it, about 5 km with no traffic lights, is the city's running loop, always run counter-clockwise.

Ekiben are bento boxes bought at the station and eaten on the train, each region's specialty in a neat box. On the bullet train people sit in their reserved seats, eat quietly and never take a phone call at the seat.

Asahina Trading is a general trading company: its people buy, sell and ship steel, grain, textiles and machinery between countries, and its forty-floor tower in Marunouchi is one of the district's best addresses. Staff call the firm "Asahina".

A depachika is a department store's basement food hall: dozens of counters of sweets, deli food, sushi, pickles and bento, with free samples and flawless wrapping. People buy gifts there, tonight's dinner, and a treat for themselves. Tsubakiya Ginza's is among the most famous.

Gifts are a duty: omiyage for colleagues after a trip, a sweets box when visiting a home, and at midsummer and year-end gifts to bosses and benefactors. The wrapping matters as much as the contents: say "for a gift" and the clerk wraps it properly.

In Ginza's flagship stores a doorman opens the door and staff bow; browsing is welcome and nobody expects a purchase. A purchase is wrapped in tissue, boxed, bagged and carried to the door. Windows change every few weeks like theater sets.

Ginza holds hundreds of small galleries, many of them free, tucked on upper floors and in basements; shows last about a week. Old counters here have sold a single item, a sponge cake or a tea, for ninety years and will say so proudly.

Izakaya Tetsuro is a one-arch izakaya under the Yūrakuchō tracks, grilled over charcoal by a master who never seems to leave the door. Asahina Trading's sections hold their year-end parties here. The first drink is beer, and the small cover dish (otoshi) shows up on the bill.

In an izakaya everyone orders a first beer at once ("toriaezu biiru"); a small otoshi dish arrives unasked and is a cover charge; plates are shared, guests pour for each other, and the bill is paid at the end. There is no tipping.

The East Gardens are the part of Edo Castle open to everyone: the huge stone base where the keep burned in 1657 and was never rebuilt, a watchtower, old walls and gates, the Ninomaru pond garden, and the Honmaru lawn. Entry is free; visitors take a token at the gate and hand it back on leaving.

Runners circle the palace counter-clockwise, 5 km without a traffic light, with distance markers every 100 meters. "Runners' stations" near the path rent lockers and showers so office workers can run after work. Pedestrians have the right of way and walkers keep to the outside.

Ginza Kabuki Hall is Ginza's kabuki theater, a single-hall house with its own revolving stage. Two shows a day, a matinee at noon and an evening show at five, change every month. Cheap gallery seats are sold at the door for cash.

Kabuki began around 1603 with a shrine maiden's dances in Kyoto; women were soon banned from the stage, so male actors called onnagata play the women's roles. The stage has a raised walkway through the audience (hanamichi), stagehands in black who are "invisible" (kuroko), and frozen poses (mie) cracked out by wooden clappers.
