Connoisseurs in the gallery shout an actor's house name (kakegoe) at the exact gap between beats, a skill of timing that takes years. Applause comes at set moments, a program explains the plot, and phones disappear.

Tsukiji's wholesale fish market, the "inner market", moved to Toyosu in 2018. The "outer market" of shops, stalls and restaurants stayed, and still sells seafood, knives, rolled omelets and sushi from dawn until early afternoon. Many shops close on Sundays and some Wednesdays.

At Tsukiji people eat at the stall, not while walking; the lanes are too narrow and shopkeepers ask politely. Knife shops engrave a name on the blade while the buyer waits. A knife given as a gift is said to cut the tie, so the receiver hands over a coin and it becomes a purchase.

Namiyoke Inari Shrine, a short walk from the lanes, is where fishmongers pray for safe seas and good trade; nearby stands the great Tsukiji Hongwanji temple, with its stone front in an Indian-inspired style. Visitors bow quietly.

Seiwa General Hospital is Marunouchi's big hospital: a white tower with a reception hall of number-ticket machines, wards of four beds and an emergency entrance on the side street that never closes. Many collapsed commuters wake up here with a drip in one arm and a nurse asking, kindly, when they last slept.

In Japan everyone carries a health insurance card: it is handed over at reception, a numbered ticket is taken, patients wait, and pay about thirty percent at the end. "Three hours of waiting for three minutes of consultation" is the joke; emergencies skip the line.

Visiting hours are afternoon and early evening. Visitors bring fruit, sweets or cut flowers, never a potted plant (the illness would "take root"), and nothing with a strong scent; some wards allow no flowers at all.

Firms send employees for an annual health check; doctors in Marunouchi see the same story every week: raised blood pressure, no sleep, skipped meals, and an apologetic patient asking whether it can wait until after the quarter.
The Marunouchi gates swallow a river of dark suits; everyone walks fast on the left with eyes on a phone, no one speaks, and train-card beeps and announcements overlap.
The last-train rush: office workers with loosened ties and red faces jog for the final trains while attendants call out departure times.
New employees in identical black suits and new shoes gather in nervous groups checking maps; seniors with company flags collect them. Everyone else on the concourse remembers being one.
The plaza market is a field of stalls on blue sheets: tea bowls, old maps, kimono fabric, rusted tools. Sellers on folding stools sip tea, and the bargaining is friendly and slow.
A cycling club in team jerseys wheeling bikes in bags, exchange students with big backpacks, couples with shopping bags; the suits are gone, and the concourse is almost cheerful.
Golden Week: the bullet-train platforms are packed, queues for unreserved seats run down the stairs, and friends and couples with bags sit on every step.
The underground streets are the only dry way anywhere: the concourse fills with people who would rather be late than wet, and the tiled floors turn slick.
The turnstiles beep without a pause: employees badge in with a coffee in one hand, bow to the guards, and ride lifts packed in silence, eyes on the floor numbers.
Lunch: lanyards flood the plaza benches, sections eat their bento together and talk shop in low voices, and the cafeteria line runs out of the door.
lore.when: place: mg_tower; period: afternoon; weekend: no

lore.content: The bell tones at six and the lights stay on. A few people leave pointedly early; most pretend not to see the clock, and the vending alcoves fill with tired people holding cans of coffee.
Whole floors are dark, but the twenty-third glows on: a few desks lit with spreadsheets and cold bento, and a cleaning crew working around people who forgot to go home.
The office gates are locked and the lobby is quiet, but the sky lobby stays open to the public until 22:00, and the weekend guard has seen every proposal photo in Marunouchi.
The air conditioning is held at a modest 28 degrees; jackets and ties come off by company rule, desk fans and cooling towels appear, and everyone looks faintly sticky.
Mei Wang sits with her tablet, red nails clicking, moving a contract between two languages and correcting both sides' grammar without looking up.
At six sharp Mei Wang leaves, announcing it in three languages, and nobody dares object: her translations hold half the section's contracts together.
lore.when: place: mg_tower; present: Mei; period: evening

lore.content: The entrance ceremony: a hundred new hires in black suits stand in rows in the atrium while the president speaks; last year's hires watch with pity and nostalgia.
The sections drift out in groups at six sharp for their year-end parties, the only night everyone leaves on time.
From about seven the clerks begin sticking red discount labels on fresh sushi, salads and bento; office workers circle the cases pretending not to wait, and boxes vanish the moment a clerk moves on.
The doors open at ten with a line of bows, the whole staff bowing to the first customers, and the air smells of sugar and grilled soy.
Couples, groups of friends and old people dressed up for the outing fill the aisles; the sample counters have queues and gift boxes are bought by the dozen.
White Day return gifts: men shop in tight packs for the right sweets, and clerks ask the one question that matters, "What is your relationship?"
Year-end gift sets stack up beside lacquered boxes of New Year food reserved weeks ago; the staff look tired and smile anyway.
Shaved ice, jelly sweets and cold noodles; the ice cream counter never stops, and midsummer gift catalogues sit by every register.

The avenue is closed to cars from noon to five: a long white line down the asphalt, chairs and big parasols in the roadway, couples and solo walkers filling it, and a steward with a whistle at every crossing.
Traffic roars down the avenue and the pavements are packed with office workers on errands, delivery carts and staff in uniforms dashing between stores.
lore.when: place: mg_chuodori; weekend: no; period: afternoon

lore.content: At eleven the shutters go up and the staff line up at each door to bow at the first customers; the street smells of floor polish.
The shops are shut and their windows glow for an almost empty street; heels echo, a few couples walk slowly, and a doorman is the last one to leave.
The windows turn pastel; men in suits carry small bags in both hands like people carrying live fish.
The early crowd is colleague groups in suits; the first round of beer arrives with the cover dish, and a section chief's speech begins before anyone has sat.
Friday night: the arch is shoulder to shoulder and the stools spill into the street; every few minutes a train shakes the beams and no one pauses a sentence.
lore.when: place: mg_izakaya; period: night; weekday: fri

lore.content: Near the last trains the groups thin out in a rush of "otsukaresama" and bows; stragglers stay on, sharing the last plates in a mood that is half confession.
Year-end party season: every table is a company or a section, the noise is a wall, and a banner by the grill gives the date; the night ends in round two, round three and many apologies.
Hot pot and warm sake are on the board; steam fogs the plastic curtain, and the grill's heat is a favor to everyone near the door.

The Thursday team drinks: the section fills the long table, Reiko Tachibana with her jacket off and her sleeves pushed up, softer than at the office, answering the jokes with one dry line, and Daisuke Mori pouring for everyone before himself.
lore.when: place: mg_izakaya; weekday: thu; period: evening; present: Reiko; present: Daisuke

lore.content: Mei Wang sits at the corner of the section's table, correcting the toasts' English and Mandarin in an undertone and leaving the Japanese ones alone.
lore.when: place: mg_izakaya; weekday: thu; period: evening; present: Mei; present: Reiko

lore.content: The East Gardens gate is shut today (the gardens close Mondays and Fridays) and guards politely send visitors back to the path; only the moat and the loop are open.
lore.when: place: mg_palace; weekday: mon or fri; period: midmorning or afternoon

lore.content: From six the path fills with office workers in running gear, headlamps and reflective bands; the pace is serious, nobody speaks, and the towers glow across the moat.
At dawn a few devoted runners and dog-walkers have the path; the moat is mist and first light turns the stone walls pink.
The Ninomaru maples and the Honmaru ginkgos turn red and gold; photographers crowd the gate at opening, and the guards hand out tokens until they run out, so it pays to arrive before ten.
Cherry trees ring the moat at Chidorigafuchi, and rowing boats slide under the petals; the path is a slow procession of phones held high.
Summer heat drives runners to dawn or dark; vending machines near the gates do brisk business, and cicadas shriek in the pines.
Rain makes the cobbles slick; only the most devoted runners remain, in bright jackets, and the gardens are nearly empty.
Daisuke Mori runs the loop in an old company T-shirt, glasses fogged, apologizing to every walker he passes.
The matinee crowd: retirees in good kimono, and couples and friends queue at the lobby counters before the opening bell; the ushers smile at everything.
lore.when: place: mg_kabuki; period: afternoon; weekend: no

lore.content: The evening crowd arrives from the offices with bento in paper bags; wooden clappers mark the first scene on the minute, and the lobby smells of tea.
The hall is full on weekends; seats on the main floor are gone by morning and only gallery seats remain.
The hall is dressed with pine and bamboo for the New Year, audiences come in kimono, and the lobby hands out small paper charms.
The market is shut for the New Year holiday: shutters down, a wreath on every door, a few cats, and no fish at all.
lore.when: place: mg_tsukiji; festival: omisoka or hatsumode

lore.content: Before dawn the lanes belong to the trade: carts, boxes of ice, steaming cups of tea, and chefs buying for the day calling to each other in clipped slang.
By eight the sushi queues wind around the corner; stall keepers hawk samples, a company outing in matching caps pours through, and a cart shouts "excuse me!" every ten steps.
lore.when: place: mg_tsukiji; period: rush or midmorning

lore.content: After one the shutters come down along the lane; hoses wash the stones, weary stall keepers eat their own breakfast, and the last visitors hunt one final omelet.
In the last days of the year people mob the market for crab, roe and New Year seafood; stall keepers shout, the lines are long and the market shuts for the holiday soon after.
Outpatient morning: the hall is a sea of numbered tickets and quiet coughing, old patients hold their cards like theater tickets, and a screen above the counter flickers through the numbers.
lore.when: place: mg_hospital; period: midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: The corridors dim to exit-sign green; night nurses move with penlights and soft shoes, the vending machines hum, and somewhere a call light chimes.
Only the emergency entrance is lit: an ambulance idling, a trolley rolling, a clerk filling out forms. The staff neither hurry nor stop.
Linh Nguyễn, a jade bracelet under her cuff, wheels the tea trolley down the ward, rehearsing polite phrases under her breath and switching to English when a word escapes her.
Linh Nguyễn eats at the end of a cafeteria table with a worn book of exam vocabulary beside her tray, mouthing the hard words and underlining them twice.
lore.when: place: mg_hospital; after: mg_hospital_cafeteria; present: Linh

lore.content: Outpatient is closed and the hall echoes; the wards are busy in the afternoon with visitors, fruit baskets and cut flowers.
Flu season: masks on everyone, sanitizer stands at each door, a vaccination poster, and an extra row of chairs in the waiting hall.
New residents in fresh white coats and new nurses in unscuffed shoes trail their seniors, trying not to look lost; the patients can tell, and are kind about it.
Year-end brings its own patients: office workers who drank too much, slipped on stairs, or simply folded at the end of a long year.
They say the cleaning crews on the Yaesu platforms turn a whole bullet train around in seven minutes, and that engineers from abroad fly in just to watch.
Antique sellers are said to draw lots for the stalls by the glass doors on the Friday before the market.
Word is Asahina's top brass will announce a reorganization before the year ends, and every section is quietly guessing which one will be merged.
People say the best-kept secret in the Asahina tower is a nap room on the twelfth floor, and that three directors have been found asleep in it.
They say the free sky lobby is a condition of the tower's building permit, and that Asahina would close it tomorrow if it could.
They say there is a melon in the fruit section priced like a week's rent for a studio, and that somebody buys one every single week.
People say the half-price hour is set by a manager who watches the cases from behind a mirror, and that he moves it by a few minutes just to keep the regulars honest.
Word is the gift wrapping costs the store more than the sweets do, and the clerks are trained for a year before they may fold a corner.
Word is the shop owners want the car-free hours cut back, because the weekend walkers look at the windows and do not buy.
They say the best window on the avenue belongs to a store nobody can enter without an introduction.
People say the cover dish here is a different small plate every night, and that the master chooses it by the weather.
Someone says the master's grandfather started on the same spot with an oden cart, and that the cart's lantern still hangs inside the door.
They say the loop has an unwritten ranking, and that the man who runs it fastest is a seventy-year-old in a faded cap who never checks his watch.
Someone says the moat's heron has a name among the regulars and disapproves of joggers.
They say the actor who plays the princess roles has done so for forty years and is still the most graceful person in Ginza.
It is said the gallery regulars can tell from the first crack of the clappers whether it will be a good night.
They say the hall's ghost is a stagehand in black who tidies the props after closing and leaves a single paper petal on the stage each time.
Locals say the best time to come is just after seven, when the buyers have gone and the visitors haven't yet arrived.
People say the seafood bowls are cheaper two lanes back, where the queues are shorter and nobody speaks English.
They say half the fourth floor is office workers who ran themselves down, and the nurses keep a quiet bet on who will be back by spring.
People say the night nurses keep a thermos of barley tea for insomniac patients and know every one of them by name.
Someone says the bench in the rooftop garden was donated by a patient who spent a whole winter up there and ended up looking after the beans.

Odaiba is a leisure island made of landfill, named after the gun batteries ("daiba") built on it in the 1850s. It has a beach, a mall, a museum and a convention center, linked by the bridge and the driverless line. It is where Tokyo goes for days out.

Toyosu, once shipyards, is now a field of fifty-story residential towers on the canals: concierge desks, gyms and sky lounges downstairs, quiet wide promenades, views across the bay. Founders, executives, heirs and quiet couples with money live here.

The bay line is an elevated driverless train from Shimbashi that curls over Rainbow Bridge and through Odaiba to Toyosu. The best seat is at the front window, where it feels like flying through the skyline. A hop costs about ¥200.

Toyosu Market has been Tokyo's wholesale fish market since 2018, when it replaced Tsukiji's inner market (the Tsukiji Outer Market, with its stalls, stayed). The tuna auction starts around 5:30. The market is closed Sundays, holidays and most Wednesdays.

The summer fan convention at the Exhibition Center fills every hall over a weekend: thousands of "circles" sell self-published comics, music and goods, cosplayers pose in a costume area, and the line starts at dawn. It is hot, huge and extremely orderly.

Wave TV Studios is a waterfront station making variety and quiz shows, morning news and idol specials. Weekday tapings seat a studio audience: numbered tickets, a warm-up comedian who drills the clapping, and the same joke on the fourth take.
Before dawn the bay is nearly empty except for the fish trucks heading for Toyosu, the first trains with a few sleepy riders, and runners in the towers' lit promenades.
The sea wind carries salt and cooking; towers glint copper and the bridge goes pink, and everyone walking the waterfront slows down to look.
lore.when: region: bay; period: evening; weather: sunny or fair

lore.content: The wind off the bay is strong and cold: scarves, hot cans from vending machines, breath clouds. Nobody lingers outside long, apart from couples and photographers.
Runners say the towers' promenades are the quietest place in Tokyo at five in the morning, as long as you keep clear of the fish trucks.

Odaiba Seaside Park is a man-made beach on reclaimed land. Swimming is banned, so people walk the sand, wade, windsurf offshore, and sit on the boardwalk steps looking across at Rainbow Bridge and the skyline. A small copy of the Statue of Liberty stands on the shore.
At sunset the skyline turns to silhouettes, the bridge lights up at dusk, and the boardwalk steps fill with people sitting in comfortable silence.
lore.when: place: bay_beach; period: evening; weather: not rain

lore.content: After dark the beach is quiet and a little romantic: the bridge and towers glitter across the water, people talk low, and a few runners pass.
A retirees' club trip photographs the statue in shifts, windsurfers are out beyond the breakwater, and a food stand sells cold drinks and grilled corn.
A cold wind comes straight off the bay; the sand is empty apart from runners in puffy coats and a few people with a thermos.
The Rainbow Bridge walkway shuts at six, so couples line the boardwalk to watch the lit bridge from the sand; photographers set up tripods, and someone plays a love song low from a speaker.
lore.when: place: bay_beach; festival: christmas; period: evening or night

lore.content: The beach empties completely; the bridge fades into grey, and a few umbrellas hurry toward the mall.
Windsurfers say the best wind comes in the hour before a storm, and the instructors never admit it.
People say that if two people watch the lit bridge together on Christmas Eve, they stay together all year, and some come back each winter to check.

Rainbow Bridge is a white suspension bridge across the bay, about 800 meters long, opened in 1993. Its free footpath, the Rainbow Promenade, is about 1.7 km from Shibaura to Odaiba on the lower deck, with a north route facing Tokyo Tower and a south route facing the bay.
The walkway closes at six in winter, so the lights are only for those who come at dusk; the wind on the span is bitter and scarves flap.
The bridge is lit white against the dark; walkers stop at the middle to look back at the skyline, and the gate closes at nine.
lore.when: place: bay_bridge; season: spring or summer or autumn; period: evening

lore.content: The walkway is closed in strong wind; a guard at the gate turns walkers back with an apologetic bow.
A few office workers on a break and a solo traveler or two walk the span; the quiet is broken only by the rumble of the highway overhead.
lore.when: place: bay_bridge; weekend: no; period: midmorning

lore.content: People feel the train humming through the railing, because the bay line runs on the same deck.
They say the guard at the Shibaura gate has counted every walker for twenty years and knows each day's number by heart.

Odaiba Harbor Mall has terraced shops, food courts and a roof terrace. In its plaza stands Kaien, a fifteen-meter white-and-teal rescue robot, hero of an old 1990s TV series. Its arm lifts and a horn sounds on the hour; its chest glows teal at night.
The Herons are Tokyo's baseball team. On game nights from spring to summer, the mall plaza hosts a public viewing: a huge screen, beer and fried chicken, navy jerseys, towels and chants in unison.
Hundreds of fans in navy jerseys fill the plaza, waving towels and chanting with the cheer squad on the screen, while Kaien's raised arm is wrapped in a team towel.
A hen party in matching sashes, exchange students and friends crowd the walkways; the food court has a wait, and Kaien's hourly salute draws a ring of raised phones.
A huge tree glows in the plaza and Kaien wears a giant red scarf; people queue to photograph each other under the raised arm.
Office workers drift in for a beer and a look at the sea; the shops thin out and the restaurants fill with after-work chatter.
lore.when: place: bay_mall; weekend: no; period: evening

lore.content: They say Kaien's horn sounds a minute late whenever the maintenance crew has had a bad week.
Fans of the old series say the statue's raised arm is the pose from episode twelve, and still argue on the plaza about whether that was the right episode.

Lumen Digital Art Museum is a warehouse on the bay of dark rooms where light is the art: paper lanterns that whisper visitors' wishes, a long table of projected meals, a hundred clocks of different cities. Entry is by timed ticket, about ¥2,800.
Timed tickets sell out by noon, the line runs down the corridor, and couples and friends whisper in the dark halls with their phones glowing.
Midweek afternoons are almost empty: a visitor can stand alone in the lantern hall and hear only their own footsteps and the lanterns' whispers.
lore.when: place: bay_art; weekend: no; period: afternoon

lore.content: The dark rooms are cool and blessedly air-conditioned; people stay much longer than the ticket suggests, to escape the heat.
Last entry is at six; the hall thins out, the lanterns shine brighter against fewer faces, and the attendants walk the corridors turning off the clocks one by one.

Camille Laurent, teal-tipped undercut and paint-spattered boots, tows Haru Aoki from room to room by the sleeve and explains what each light "means"; Haru, silver ear cuffs catching the glow, answers in one dry word and sketches the lantern hall in a pocket notebook when they think nobody is looking.
lore.when: place: bay_art; weekday: sun; period: afternoon; present: Haru; present: Camille

lore.content: They say one clock in the clock room shows the wrong time on purpose, and the staff won't say which.
People say the whispers in the lantern hall are never deleted, and the oldest was recorded on opening day.

The Tokyo Bay Exhibition Center is a huge convention complex whose conference tower is an upside-down pyramid. Its halls hold a different fair most weeks: food, interiors, weddings, robots, pets. It is reached by the bay line or the waterfront rail line.

The summer fan convention fills every hall over a weekend: two days when thousands of "circles" sell self-published comics, music and goods; cosplayers pose in a costume area; the line starts at dawn. Everyone carries their own trash out, and nobody pushes.

The Tokyo ramen contest fills one hall on a summer day: forty cooks from shops all over the city serve small tasting bowls to a paying crowd and a panel of judges in white aprons; the winning bowl is painted on a sign at the entrance for a year.
A trade fair is on: salespeople in matching jackets hand out samples, and buyers with lanyards wander between booths with tote bags.
lore.when: place: bay_expo; weekend: no; period: midmorning or afternoon

lore.content: Lines of tens of thousands snake around the plaza from the first train; cosplayers pose by the fountains, the halls are a crush of paper bags, and the bay line is packed to the doors.
The heat turns the plaza into a furnace: staff hand out water, and cosplayers in heavy armor retreat to the cooling stations between photos.
lore.when: place: bay_expo; festival: fancon; period: afternoon; weather: hot or sunny

lore.content: A hobby fair draws enthusiasts: model builders, board-game players, craft sellers and collectors, all very polite and very serious.
lore.when: place: bay_expo; weekend: yes; festival: not fancon

lore.content: Cooks in matching aprons man booths along one hall, each with a pot, a paper number and a line of people with tasting cups; the judges walk the rows without smiling, and the crowd votes with wooden tokens.

Ayaka Kamei, bandana tied tight and an apron over a band tee, ladles tiny bowls of her own broth at a booth near the back, glancing at the entrance every few minutes as if someone might walk in; she has told almost nobody she is here.
lore.when: place: bay_expo; festival: ramen_contest; present: Ayaka

lore.content: Kanon Shiraishi, her table in the hall (her yearly place at the convention, both days), sits at the back under a hand-lettered sign, her sketchbook flat in front of her, more people at her table than she expected; she is mumbling prices and avoiding eyes, and it is the one weekend a year she leaves her apartment for more than a convenience-store run.
lore.when: place: bay_expo; festival: fancon; present: Kanon

lore.content: Between buyers, Kanon watches the aisle for a woman in an oversized gaming hoodie who bought her book last year, and brightens at every hoodie that isn't hers.
lore.when: place: bay_expo; festival: fancon; present: Kanon; chance: 0.5

lore.content: People say the first in line at the summer convention arrives at midnight, though security insists nobody is allowed to.
They say the circles at the far end of the east hall sell the rarest books, because most buyers are worn out before they reach them.

Toyosu Market is Tokyo's wholesale fish market, open since 2018 when it replaced the inner market at Tsukiji. The halls are enclosed and cold; visitors watch the tuna auction and the work floor from glass galleries. It is closed Sundays, holidays and most Wednesdays.

The tuna auction starts around 5:30. Fresh and frozen tuna lie numbered on the floor, each cut at the tail so buyers can judge it by flashlight. Buyers bid with flicks of the fingers; the winner's mark goes on the fish, and trucks haul it away.
Turret trucks are small three-wheeled carts with the driver on a swivel seat, weaving through the halls at speed. Visitors are told to stay on the walkways and never in the lane.
The auction hall roars with bells and shouting; turret trucks weave between rows of tuna as buyers bid with a flick of the fingers.
lore.when: place: bay_market; event: tuna; period: firsttrain

lore.content: By noon the floors are hosed down and the shutters are coming down; a few workers eat noodles standing up, and the gallery is empty.
The halls are kept cold: a chill hits at the door, and workers wear fleeces under their aprons even in July.
Before the New Year, restaurants' orders are huge; the halls are packed with buyers and the work runs long.
The year's first auction: a giant bluefin sells for an absurd price in front of TV cameras; the gallery is packed, and the price is more good-luck show than market price.
The market is closed: gates shut, a guard on duty, and a lone driver eating at a vending machine; only the rooftop garden is open.
lore.when: place: bay_market; weekday: sun or wed

lore.content: They say an old buyer hasn't missed a morning in thirty years and can tell a tuna's age by tapping it.
People say the year's first tuna is bought more for the cameras than for the fish.

Wave TV Studios is a waterfront station making variety shows, quiz shows, morning news and idol specials. The lobby has a wave sculpture and a gift shop; guests arrive by the stage door on the harbor side, where fans wait.

A studio audience gets numbered tickets, is seated by an assistant director, and is drilled by a warm-up comedian in when to clap, when to gasp and how to laugh at the same joke on its fourth take. Phones are checked at the door.

Idols are booked on variety shows to grow: they play games, taste food and answer questions. Hanabira Signal, five women from the small Stage Starlight theater in Akihabara, are a rising name at Wave TV; the top of an idol's career is on television.
The audience queue winds around the plaza with numbered tickets; a warm-up comedian works the line and assistants shout instructions through megaphones.
Live shows are being prepped: the corridors fill with runners, makeup carts and rolling flight cases, and red lights glow over the studio doors.
The late-night variety studio is full of music and laughter; the canteen sells instant noodles, and the crew look gray and cheerful.
Tours run on the hour and the gift shop sells towels and mugs with show logos, but most studios are dark and quiet.

Hina Asano, in a plain cap and a mask, waits in the corridor outside a studio for her monthly guest slot with Hanabira Signal, both hands around a paper cup; passing staff bow to her without breaking stride.
lore.when: place: bay_tv; event: tv_taping; present: Hina

lore.content: They say a dating show was pulled when the contestants really fell in love and stopped doing the show's tasks.
People say the weather forecaster is the station's real star: viewers send her handwritten letters, and the network fears she'll quit.
They say Hanabira Signal will get a weekly spot if their next single holds up.
The tower lobby is silent apart from the concierge's keyboard; down the canal the first fish trucks rumble toward the market, and runners pass along the promenade in the dark.
lore.when: zone: hz_toyosu; period: latenight or firsttrain

lore.content: The sky lounge fills with residents in loose clothes, laptops open and drinks untouched, looking out over the bay while the bridge lights come on one by one.
The concierge greets {{user}} by the family name and says the flat is "as always"; Rina Tachibana's floor is two above, and the staff already know the two families are acquainted.

Rina Tachibana sits alone at the sky lounge's long table with two phones face-up and a laptop open, the bridge lights behind her; she nods to the concierge, who nods back, and neither of them mentions the hour.
lore.when: zone: hz_toyosu; present: Rina; period: night

lore.content: Jake Miller, in a flannel shirt and a minor-league cap, comes through the lobby with a grocery bag and a laptop under one arm, greets the concierge in cheerful terrible Japanese, and says he lives a few floors below Rina's.
lore.when: zone: hz_toyosu; present: Jake; period: evening or night

lore.content: Roppongi is Tokyo's international nightlife district. Its crossing sits under an expressway, where two avenues meet, and is the meeting spot for clubbers, visitors and taxis. By day it is offices, galleries and quiet; the party starts after dark and runs until the first train at five.

Touts in Roppongi pull people into bars with "free drink" cards. A few venues overcharge (bottakuri) or drug drinks to rob people; the police patrol, and foreign embassies keep warning about it. Locals' rules: ignore touts, keep a drink in one's own hand, never follow a stranger's card, go out in a group.

Tokyo Tower is a 333-meter steel tower painted orange and white, opened in 1958. It has a main deck at 150 meters and a top deck at 250, and is lit every night from sunset until midnight. At its foot lie Zōjō-ji, the Tokugawa family's great temple, and Shiba Park.

Azabu-Jūban is a shopping street about three hundred years old that grew in front of Zenpuku-ji's gate. Its station opened only in 2000, so locals called the area "the island". Bakeries, soba shops and a taiyaki stall (the fish-shaped pastry is said to have been born here) sit below some of Tokyo's priciest flats.

Meridian Hills is a tower-and-garden complex of offices, flats and shops near the crossing. Its top floors hold the Sky Museum: an art museum with a glass-walled deck over the whole city. Several other museums sit within a few minutes' walk.

Roppongi and Azabu are where many embassies, diplomats and foreign residents live and drink. English is heard in bars, pubs and cafés, and staff often switch language mid-sentence. Japanese is still the default everywhere else, and the same rules of manners apply to everyone.

lore.when: place: rp_crossing; period: night; weekend: yes
lore.content: Friday and Saturday the crossing is the party: bass leaks from every basement, taxis queue nose to tail, groups pose for photos under the expressway, and touts hold fistfuls of flyers. Police stand in pairs at the corners.

By half past midnight the last trains are gone and the crossing becomes the city's taxi rank. Fares carry the night surcharge, couples split cars, and people waiting for the first train eat at the kebab cart and watch the sky pale.

lore.when: place: rp_crossing; period: midmorning or afternoon
lore.content: By day it is a plain junction: office workers, delivery vans, a few early visitors. The doorways touts use are shuttered and the expressway's concrete looks heavier without neon.
The avenues leading away from the crossing glow in blue-white light tunnels. Couples and sightseers walk slowly under them, and even the touts are in a good mood.
The expressway keeps the crossing half dry, so everyone bunches under it: umbrellas queue at the lights, taxis are scarce, and touts wear clear plastic ponchos over the same dark coats.
They say the police have been out in force and the touts have moved from the crossing into the side streets, which is somehow worse.
A friend of a friend woke on a bench at dawn with no wallet and no memory past a free drink.
Everyone agrees the best Roppongi night ends at the kebab cart, watching the first train's sun come up.

Saturday's big night: the line runs around the block from ten, the main floor opens at eleven, and three DJs share a bill that runs to five. Staff wear radios; the roof terrace stays full of people trading bits of the night.

lore.when: place: rp_club; period: night; weekday: wed or thu
lore.content: Weeknights are half-empty: regulars, DJs trying out new sets, cheap drinks, nobody pushing a bottle. A person who wants to learn the club's staff or its music has the room to do it.

lore.when: place: rp_club; period: night; weekday: sun
lore.content: Sunday is guest DJ night: only the lounge floor is open, people come in from other nights to listen instead of dance, and the room is gone by one.
From half past four the floor thins. People in sunglasses squint from the roof terrace at the dawn, the cleaners start at the stairs, and a sleepy line heads for the five o'clock train.

lore.when: place: rp_club; present: Lisa; weekday: sun
lore.content: Lisa Morimoto is the Sunday guest DJ, on her night off from Pole Star. She plays in streetwear and keeps one eye on the door for friends.
They say a famous DJ from abroad turned up unannounced last month and played ninety minutes on the lounge floor before anyone noticed.
The main floor's sound is tuned to one spot marked with a tape cross, and the resident DJs argue over who may stand on it.
The door staff say they can tell who will cause trouble from the way someone holds their drink.

After sunset the deck gives the city's best night view: a carpet of lights to the horizon, red beacons blinking on every tower, Tokyo Tower glowing orange nearby. People speak quietly and stay longer than they planned.
The galleries close at seven but the deck stays open until late. Guards herd the last art visitors out as the deck fills with people who came for the view.

lore.when: place: rp_sky; season: winter; weather: fujiview; period: midmorning or afternoon
lore.content: On a clear winter day Mt. Fuji floats on the western horizon, and the deck fills with people holding phones toward it.
The Sky Museum is closed on Tuesdays; the lifts are switched off and the shop's windows are dark.

lore.when: place: rp_sky; present: Mei; weekday: wed; period: evening
lore.content: Mei Wang stands alone at the deck's glass on Wednesday evenings, tablet under her arm, murmuring to herself in Mandarin as the lights come on. She is thinking, not waiting, and answers company with dry, precise politeness.

lore.when: place: rp_sky; present: Mei; weekday: wed; period: evening; feels: Mei friend
lore.content: Tonight Mei's murmuring is a rehearsal: one interview question in three languages, answered again and again until the phrasing is exact. If {{user}} comes close she stops mid-sentence and says it is a presentation for work; she does not say for which company.
People say a pair got stuck in the deck elevator for twenty minutes and came out having swapped numbers, apologies and a long argument about a painting.
The guards swear one painting changes its mood with the light, and there is a bench for people who need to sit with it.
Every evening the lights come on at sunset and stay on until midnight; on some nights special lighting plays across the lattice. The deck goes quiet for it, and people wait without saying so.
On Christmas Eve the deck is full of couples and the tower wears special lights; the staff have seen it all and pretend not to notice.
Cherry trees around Zōjō-ji and in Shiba Park frame the tower in pink; picnic blankets cover the lawns and the Main Deck windows are full of pale petals.
They say a crew of painters hangs on the lattice for months, repainting it orange and white every five years, and that nobody has ever seen them come down.
People say that if two people watch the lights go out at midnight from the Main Deck, they stay together.

lore.when: place: rp_azabu; period: midmorning or afternoon
lore.content: Bakers carry trays, old women push shopping carts, and embassy staff buy bread and flowers on their way home. The shopkeepers call regulars by name and ask after relatives.
Weekends bring day-trippers and foreign residents with tote bags. The taiyaki line wraps around the corner, and old residents complain gently while standing in it.
By nine the shutters are down; a few izakaya, a konbini and the glow of Tokyo Tower are all that's left. The street is so quiet that footsteps carry, and anyone late is easily noticed.
The ginkgo at Zenpuku-ji turns gold, the street fills with people carrying cameras, and the baker sells bread rolls shaped like fallen leaves.

The summer night market fills the street with stalls and lanterns. Food stalls come from embassy kitchens, shopkeepers cook outdoors and much of the neighborhood turns out in yukata. It runs two nights, and the crowd is huge.

lore.when: place: rp_azabu; present: Shōta; period: afternoon
lore.content: Out of his suit, in plain clothes, Shōta Asano is the quiet man on the bench by the taiyaki stand, eating one and watching the street like he's off duty for once.
People here still call the neighborhood "the island", from the years before the station, and the old shopkeepers say that's why the street kept its manners.
The taiyaki here is said to be older than the tower, and two stalls have argued about who makes it best for longer than that.
The shopkeepers' unwritten rule is that nobody raises prices before the Noryō, and the one who did got a quiet visit from the neighbors.
Dim amber light, the tower orange in the glass, and conversations that drop to a hush when the lights change. Nobody here raises their voice, and nobody checks the price.
At six the lounge has just opened: one bartender polishing glasses, the window tables free, and the best chance of a seat without a reservation.

lore.when: place: rp_lounge; weekday: fri; period: night
lore.content: Friday is the closing night for deals: business owners and investors, the host turning walk-ins away at the door, and the window tables long booked.

lore.when: place: rp_lounge; present: Rina; period: night
lore.content: Rina Tachibana sits at the corner table with two phones face-down, pitching with a smile. Her eyes are tired, but she makes sure nobody notices.

lore.when: place: rp_lounge; present: Airi; period: night
lore.content: Airi Mizusawa takes the end of the bar in a designer coat and sunglasses, laughs across the room in Osaka dialect and tips the bartender well. She comes because the bartender asks no questions. Nobody should ask about her work.

lore.when: place: rp_lounge; present: Airi; present: Momo; weekday: thu; period: night
lore.content: Thursday is Airi's night with Momo Sakuraba: a booth by the window, Airi ordering for both and telling the bartender in Osaka dialect that the rookie gets one cocktail and no more, Momo laughing and then asking something serious about contracts.

lore.when: place: rp_lounge; present: Airi; feels: Airi friend; period: night
lore.content: Airi keeps a small paper calendar in her coat pocket with one date circled; her agency has not been told. To someone she trusts she says, lightly, that she has a last day in mind and wants a bar of her own after it, and asks that it stay between them.
There is no menu at the Ninth Floor; the bartender prices each drink to the guest, and nobody has ever asked what the system is.
The lounge's regular list is a sealed book, and people say a name in it can open doors across Tokyo.

lore.when: place: rp_pub; weekday: sun; period: afternoon
lore.content: Sunday roast: the kitchen sells out of beef by four, football shirts fill the room and expats talk about home.
Chloe Bennett has the end of the bar, a pint going flat beside her and an argument about football or the weather already under way.
Lisa Morimoto stops by in streetwear before heading across the street. She never stays for a whole pint, and tells whoever is nearest to come along.

Lucas Oliveira, the exchange student behind the bar in a football shirt, pours with a flourish and flirts with the whole room in two languages. When Chloe Bennett is at the bar he pours her pint without being asked and argues the match with her.
Jake Miller fills a corner chair too small for him, a minor-league cap on the table, calling everyone "buddy" and keeping the quiz team's scorecard like it is a spreadsheet.

lore.when: place: rp_pub; weekday: tue; present: Jake; present: Chloe; period: night
lore.content: On quiz night Jake Miller's team and Chloe Bennett's are old rivals, trading groans and fake threats across two pushed-together tables; the loser buys the winner's first drink.

lore.when: place: rp_pub; present: Jake; feels: Jake friend; period: night
lore.content: Between rounds Jake's phone buzzes face-down on the table, a long number starting +1. He turns it over, reads it and puts it back without answering; if {{user}} asks, he says it is "just home" and orders another round, and does not say what home wants.

lore.when: place: rp_pub; weekday: tue; period: night
lore.content: Quiz night, from nine: teams of regulars at pushed-together tables, a quizmaster with a microphone, scorecards, and groans that carry into the street. The prize is a round.

lore.when: place: rp_pub; weekend: yes; period: night
lore.content: The pub is packed: staff pass drinks overhead, pre-club groups arrive and leave around midnight toward the crossing, and the football crowd sings.
The last-orders bell goes at half past midnight. Regulars drift to the crossing, those who missed the last train look for a taxi, and the landlord stacks stools with the radio on low.
They say the landlord's friend flew in a barrel of real ale last week, and it was gone in a night.
Word is an embassy team has won three quizzes in a row, and nobody wants to say how.
The regulars swear the dartboard's double top is a hair wider than regulation, and that the landlord knows.

The stage is blue and the room is quiet between songs. Applause is clapping, not shouting. The house rules are strict and enforced: no touching, no photographs, and no following a dancer out of the door.

lore.when: place: rp_poleclub; weekday: wed or sat; period: afternoon
lore.content: Class afternoons: the poles are chalked, the music is a metronome, and office workers, a retired ballet teacher and friends in borrowed shorts all take turns at the first spin. The class is part of the club, so it is adult only.

lore.when: place: rp_poleclub; weekday: wed; period: afternoon; present: Momo
lore.content: Momo Sakuraba, tall and athletic from years of volleyball, is in the front row of the class, apologizing every time she slips and getting back up grinning. Lisa Morimoto cheers her on by name.

lore.when: place: rp_poleclub; weekday: wed or sat; period: afternoon; present: Lisa
lore.content: Lisa Morimoto runs the pole-fitness class herself on class afternoons: chalk on her hands, a loud count, and no mercy for anyone who skips the warm-up.

lore.when: place: rp_poleclub; weekend: yes; period: night
lore.content: Saturday is the full show: the room is full of groups of friends, office parties and a line of tippers, and the manager keeps a close eye on the floor.
After the last show the dancers peel off their tape and the manager walks them to the taxi stand in pairs. The bartender mops, and the poles stay in the dark.
They say Pole Star began as a fitness studio, and the owner moved the poles downstairs when the rent went up.
A former dancer opened her own studio in Setagaya last year, and half the class followed her.
Some regulars have come for years and never learned a dancer's real name; the dancers like it that way.

lore.when: zone: hz_azabu; period: evening or night
lore.content: The concierge at the desk nods to everyone who comes in and notes, without comment, who comes in late. The lobby smells of flowers and floor polish, and the lift hums up to flats where Tokyo Tower fills every window.

lore.when: zone: hz_azabu; weekday: sun; period: evening; present: Shōta; present: Hina
lore.content: Sunday dinner at the Asano flat: Shōta in plain clothes cooking something from home in Niigata, Hina with her cap and mask finally off, the two of them talking over each other about nothing. It is the one evening neither works.
Airi Mizusawa lives on an upper floor, in sunglasses even in the lift. The concierge greets her by name and has been told to say nothing about her visitors.

Yokohama is Japan's biggest port city, forty minutes from Tokyo. It opened to foreign ships in the 1850s, which is why it has Japan's biggest Chinatown, old trading-house streets and a mix of everything. Locals call themselves Hamakko ("port people"): a little proud, a little rough and very loyal.

Minato Mirai ("Port of the Future") is the glossy waterfront: a giant Ferris wheel with a clock face, tall towers, the old red-brick customs warehouses turned into shops and event halls, and a promenade along the bay. At night it belongs to couples.

Isezakichō is the shopping street a few minutes from the station: more than a kilometer of arcades, diners, pawn shops, secondhand bookstores, pachinko halls and tiny bars, with a car-free stretch called Isezaki Mall. Its diners serve napolitan, spaghetti in ketchup sauce, a dish Yokohama claims to have invented.

Noge is a maze of narrow alleys full of tiny izakaya and standing bars near Sakuragichō station, by the Ōoka River, where an evening costs less than anywhere in the city. Counters are shared and strangers talk. Each April its street-performance festival fills the alleys, and audiences pay by tossing coins.

The Hamakaze Group, named for the wind off the bay, lends money to people the banks turn away. Its underworld ties are known to everyone and said by nobody. Its collectors are polite, arrive on time and wait. A rival outfit from across the river is just as unnamed.

Ichō Park, named for its ginkgo trees, is a small park near Isezaki where about a dozen people without homes live and look out for each other: the Professor (once a technical-college lecturer), the herb woman (a restaurant cook until it closed), the sweeper (an old dockworker) and the cat feeder. Neighbors nod to them by name.

Weekend afternoons the main street is a slow river of retirees on club trips, couples and old friends, every bun stall with a line, every restaurant host calling out menus in two languages. Walking is a shuffle.
lore.when: place: yk_chinatown; period: midmorning or afternoon; weekend: yes

lore.content: The lanterns come on. Restaurants glow orange behind steamed windows, round tables fill with office parties and friends, and cooks shout orders across open kitchens while garlic and sesame drift down every lane.
lore.when: place: yk_chinatown; period: evening or night

lore.content: A lion dance moves through the streets: drums echoing off the gates, shopkeepers hanging red envelopes and lettuce from their doors for the lion to take, firecracker paper in the gutters.

At the temple door incense burns in a big bronze urn. People bow three times and ask for good business and loyal friends, and the fortune tellers' tables outside trade steadily in the other kind of luck.
lore.when: place: yk_chinatown; period: afternoon or evening; weekend: no

lore.content: Before the lunch rush, old women wash vegetables in bins on the pavement, delivery bikes squeeze past the gates, and cooks smoke at back doors. The street is quiet in the way a kitchen is quiet.
lore.when: place: yk_chinatown; period: midmorning; weekend: no

lore.content: They say the fortune teller by the east gate has never been wrong, and that she charges less the more she is sure.
Cooks say the lanterns over the main gates are re-hung by hand every New Year, one rope at a time, by the same four shopkeepers.
The warehouses hold a Christmas market: wooden stalls, mulled wine, a tall lit tree. Couples hold paper cups and breathe clouds, and the Ferris wheel is the most expensive place to be warm.
lore.when: place: yk_bay; period: evening or night; season: winter; seasonDays: 1-4

lore.content: Friday and Saturday nights the promenade is full of couples on benches, groups taking photos with the wheel behind them, and friends sitting on the stone edge with convenience-store beer.
lore.when: place: yk_bay; period: night; weekend: yes

lore.content: On the clearest days the bay sparkles and Mount Fuji shows as a pale shape on the far western horizon, for anyone who knows where to look.
Office workers cross the promenade at a march on the way to the towers, coffee in hand, while joggers loop the bay and the wheel stands still.
lore.when: place: yk_bay; period: rush; weekend: no

lore.content: Harbor workers say the horns are timed: the white ship at six sounds longer than any of the others, and nobody has ever said why.
Shopkeepers say a brick in the oldest warehouse wall has a name scratched into it from 1913, and nobody has matched it to anyone.
Wedding couples pose with the liner behind them, followed by photographers, parents and a friend holding a veil against the wind. The seawall is lined with onlookers who applaud now and then.
lore.when: place: yk_yamashita; weekend: yes; period: midmorning or afternoon

lore.content: The rose beds are in bloom, red, yellow, pink and white along the promenade. People kneel in the paths for photos and old men argue over which rose is best.
After dark the liner is lit in rows of tiny lights, the benches are full of couples, and a lone busker plays something slow on a saxophone.
Collectors say the liner's ticket window once sold a postcard with the ship's name misspelled, and that one now fetches ¥3,000 at a flea market.

Weekday afternoons the arcade belongs to the neighborhood: old men on benches, shopkeepers sweeping, women with shopping bags, and the pachinko halls already roaring with regulars who have been there since opening.
lore.when: place: yk_isezaki; period: afternoon; weekend: no

lore.content: The neon wakes up; tiny bars light their signs up the stairs, and pachinko doors rattle open on rock and bells. Work crowds mix with the old regulars, and the buskers play louder.
lore.when: place: yk_isezaki; period: evening or night

lore.content: The covered arcade keeps the rain off, so the whole neighborhood ducks in at once: umbrellas pile up in shop doorways, the pavement is a traffic jam, and the buskers finally have an audience.
Shopkeepers stand outside with steaming trays of fried snacks, a truck sells roasted sweet potato, and in the evening the arcade smells of oil and smoke.
Everyone says a pawn shop in Isezaki once took a pair of old boots that turned out to be a famous singer's, and the broker never sold them.
They say a diner in the arcade has made napolitan the same way since the sixties and throws out anyone who asks for cheese on it.
Word is one pachinko hall keeps a free tea corner, and the tea is better than the machines' odds.
Counters seat five or six. Strangers share elbows, and owners introduce neighbors whether they like it or not. Everyone has a good story about the alley, and everyone tells it.
lore.when: place: yk_noge; period: evening or night

lore.content: Weekend afternoons the first doors open at noon, and old regulars drink in their weekday suits: former dockworkers and grandfathers telling stories with their eyes closed.
lore.when: place: yk_noge; period: afternoon; weekend: yes

lore.content: On Sunday nights, once the batting cages are dark and the club is closed, two women take the end of one counter: the tall one in a track jacket eats everything on the other's plate between insults, and the one with the folded fan pretends to mind and orders more. The owner sets out a second plate without being asked.
lore.when: place: yk_noge; present: Sayuri; present: Akane; weekday: sun; period: night

lore.content: The street-performance festival fills every alley: jugglers, clowns, musicians, a one-man play. Audiences throw coins to pay (nagesen), and the whole neighborhood is a stage.
Word is a three-stool bar in Noge takes its first round in songs, not yen, and the regulars have a list of who owes one.
They say an old detective drinks at the oldest counter and will name the bars that water the whisky, for the price of a skewer.

Half the sofas are empty even on a Friday. Sayuri works the room herself, fan in hand: a word at every table, a laugh at the right moment, the faded mural behind her. The house rule is no touching, and the doorman enforces it.
lore.when: place: yk_hostess; present: Sayuri; period: night

lore.content: On weeknights the room is nearly empty and the hostesses sing to each other to pass the time. Sayuri says quiet nights pay the rent, and loud ones pay for everything else.
lore.when: place: yk_hostess; period: night; weekend: no

lore.content: Once a month, on a Friday, a polite man in a gray suit takes the window table, orders oolong tea and waits. Sayuri's smile does not change, but her fan stops moving. He leaves a tip at the door.
lore.when: place: yk_hostess; onShift: Sayuri; weekday: fri; period: night; chance: 0.25; feels: Sayuri friend

lore.content: They say the Group has been asking about Club Hibiscus's lease, and that Sayuri has stopped answering the question.
lore.when: region: yokohama; season: autumn or winter; chance: 0.2

lore.content: Word is Club Hibiscus has the longest karaoke list in Isezaki, and the mama knows the words to every song on it.
Floodlights turn the lot white. Office workers swing in their work shirts, a salaryman near the end cage hits one ball for every year of his career, and Akane yells advice from the bench.
lore.when: place: yk_batting; period: evening or night

lore.content: Weekend afternoons the cages fill with friends, couples and old teammates daring each other to try the fast machine. Anyone who rings the board gets a free can of coffee.
lore.when: place: yk_batting; period: afternoon; weekend: yes

lore.content: On the wall behind the counter hangs a faded satin jacket in a plastic cover, embroidered with a motorcycle and a name. Akane says it's a customer's.
lore.when: place: yk_batting; present: Akane; feels: Akane friend

lore.content: They say the woman who runs Home Run Alley once led a motorbike gang that ruled the bay road, and that's why nobody argues with her.
Word is a salaryman swings there every night at midnight, in full suit, for the same twenty minutes, and nobody has asked why.

Six tables run the tournament, each with a hand-written bracket; spectators press along the rail and the master leaves the counter for the head table. By midnight it's down to eight players and silence.
On ordinary nights the clatter of tiles is a kind of rain. Four men play at table two, three women at table four, and nobody speaks except to call a tile.
lore.when: place: yk_mahjong; period: night; event: not mahjong_night

lore.content: Early on, the first tables fill with retirees on their way home; they play slowly, pour tea, talk about knees and the weather, and leave by eight.
They say the master of Parlor Tenpai was once a professional player and gave it up after a hand he won and shouldn't have.
Word is the old woman at table four has not lost a hand in this parlor in six years, and does not look at her tiles.
Some say a back room at the end of the stairs plays for real money. The master says it's a storage closet.
The camp is tidy. Tents are folded or aired, someone sweeps, someone waters a row of potted herbs, and a neighbor hands over bread from the bakery that's a day past its date.
lore.when: place: yk_park; period: rush or midmorning

lore.content: A camp stove under the bandstand, a pot of stew, five or six people passing bowls. One reads aloud from a day-old newspaper and the others argue about it.
lore.when: place: yk_park; period: evening or night

lore.content: In storms they gather under the bandstand roof and shelter together with tarps tied, and the neighborhood brings tea and blankets. It is a rule that nobody is left alone in bad weather.
lore.when: place: yk_park; weather: rain or storm

lore.content: The ginkgo trees turn gold and the path is covered in yellow leaves; the sweeper leaves some for the cat feeder's photos and the neighborhood comes to look. The smell is a little rank and everyone loves it anyway.
They say the Professor of Ichō Park once designed harbor cranes, and still corrects the pilots' mistakes from memory.
Word is the herb woman cooked for half of Isezaki at a restaurant that closed in the nineties, and has never told anyone her old name.
Everyone in the neighborhood knows that anyone looking for someone in Isezaki can ask in the park, because the park notices everything.

Hakone is a mountain resort about 90 minutes from Shinjuku on a reserved-seat limited express (the front seats with the glass nose are the ones everyone wants). Hakone-Yumoto is the gate; day-trippers ride the mountain railway, cable car and ropeway, then cross Lake Ashi by boat. Travelers bring omiyage, onsen manju and wooden mosaic boxes, back for colleagues.

Onsen etiquette: guests undress in the changing room and take the small towel to the bath area, sit on a stool and wash everything with soap before entering, and tie up long hair. The small towel stays on the head or the bath's edge, never in the water. No swimsuits, no phones, no splashing. Baths are split by gender.

Many onsen refuse visible tattoos, because of old ties to gangs; it is each bath's own rule, not the law, and some now allow small ones under a skin-tone seal. The usual way around it is a private bath (kashikiri), booked by the half hour: nobody else is in the room, so friends and couples can bathe together.

A ryokan is a traditional inn. The okami (proprietress) greets guests at the door; a room attendant (nakai) brings tea and a sweet to a tatami room. Guests wear the yukata (left side over right), eat a multi-course kaiseki dinner, and staff lay futon on the floor while they eat or bathe. Check-in is mid-afternoon, check-out by ten.

Mt. Fuji shows from Lake Ashi and Ōwakudani only on clear days, mostly winter and autumn mornings before cloud gathers; from June to September haze usually hides it. Everyone in Hakone checks the sky at breakfast, and "it's out today" is a reason to change plans.

Hakone sits on an active volcano. Around Ōwakudani, sulfur dioxide sometimes rises with the wind, and the ropeway stops until the readings fall; buses take over. People with asthma or heart conditions are told to stay away from the valley on those days. It is routine, not alarming.

Hakone-Yumoto is the gateway station of Hakone: the express from Shinjuku stops here, and the little red mountain railway climbs from here in switchbacks to Gora. The shopping street leads to the Hayakawa river, with onsen manju, wooden mosaic crafts and hot-spring inns along it.
Day-trippers and a company outing in matching lanyards crowd the street with wheeled bags; the bun counters have a line and shopkeepers hand out samples on toothpicks.
lore.when: place: hk_yumoto; period: midmorning or afternoon; weekend: yes

lore.content: The shops have shut, the street is quiet, and the light shifts to the ryokan across the river; the last day-trippers wait for the train, and the air smells of steam and sulfur.
Late cherry trees along the Hayakawa are in flower; petals float on the brown river and people stop on the bridge for photographs.
Hydrangeas line the mountain tracks in blue and violet; the evening train runs with its carriages lit, and every platform bench is full of people waiting for it.
Steam from the bun counters and the vents fogs the cold air; people hold hot buns in both hands to warm them.

Rina and Shizuka stroll the shopping street like old friends: one bag of manju between them, a hand's width apart, laughing a little too easily. In public they keep it discreet, since the neighbors know every ryokan family; they drop the act only with someone they trust.
lore.when: place: hk_yumoto; period: afternoon; present: Rina; present: Shizuka; feels: Rina friend

lore.content: Locals say the manju shop at the top of the street, the one with no sign, has used the same bean paste for ninety years and will tell no one the secret.

Ryokan Kasumi-sō is a family inn of eight rooms on a steep lane above the Hayakawa, run by the Kasumi family for four generations. The okami greets every guest at the door; her daughter Shizuka is the heir and works the floor. Its outdoor bath of rock lies under old cedars.
Dinner is served in the rooms. The nakai kneel at the door with trays, name each dish, and slide away; by the end of the course the futon has been laid on the tatami while the guests were eating.
Snow settles on the stones of the outdoor bath; steam rolls into the black air, and guests soak with snow melting on their hair. The corridors are warmed with heaters, and the tea is stronger.
The maples around the garden are red and the house is booked months ahead; the okami turns away walk-ins at the door with a bow and the name of a neighbor who may have a room.
The ryokan is full: extra tea sets, a line at the baths, and Shizuka moving between rooms without a free breath, her smile never slipping.
lore.when: place: hk_ryokan; festival: goldenweek or hatsumode

lore.content: Breakfast trays go out at 7:30, the men's and women's baths swap sides, and guests check out by ten with luggage in the lobby, bowing to the okami at the door.
Midweek the house is half empty: the nakai have time to chat, and the okami may sit with a guest over tea.
At work Shizuka is her mother's shadow: kimono, tight bun, never sitting, never raising her voice.
A flicker crosses Shizuka's face when the phone at the desk rings, and she answers it herself, always. With someone she trusts she lets slip that she is tired of being polite for a living.
lore.when: place: hk_ryokan; present: Shizuka; feels: Shizuka friend

lore.content: The okami has begun to say one suitor's family name at every meal, as if the matter were settled. Shizuka answers "yes, Mother" to everything and carries trays faster.
lore.when: place: hk_ryokan; season: autumn; present: Shizuka; feels: Shizuka friend

lore.content: New Year is near and an answer is due. Shizuka has stopped smiling at the desk when no guest is looking, and she takes her tea at the garden door, in the cold, alone.
lore.when: place: hk_ryokan; season: winter; present: Shizuka; feels: Shizuka friend

lore.content: For a couple staying together, the nakai do not knock once the futon is laid and the lights are low: a ryokan is discreet, and the corridor is quiet except for the hot-spring pipes. Breakfast is simply served for two.
lore.when: place: hk_ryokan; period: night; companion: dating; after: hk_ryokan_dinner

lore.content: Staff at the other inns say Shizuka has started taking the early express to Tokyo on her days off, always in jeans, and never says why.
Guests swear the outdoor bath at Kasumi-sō is hotter on nights when it snows; the cook says it is only that the guests are colder.

Lake Ashi fills an old volcanic crater. At Moto-Hakone, Hakone Shrine (founded in 757) stands among cedars; its red Peace Torii rises from the water, put up in 1952. Photographers queue to shoot it, and on clear days Mt. Fuji stands behind it. A cedar avenue of the old Tōkaidō road runs along the shore.
Mt. Fuji is out: a white cap above the far hills, sharp in the cold air. People stop on the shore mid-sentence, and phones come out all along the line.
Mt. Fuji is lost in haze; the boat guides say "it's there, you just can't see it." The gate stands in pale water and the cedars drip.
lore.when: place: hk_ashi; weather: not fujiview; season: summer

lore.content: The torii queue wraps along the shore, couples in matching coats and a cycling group in bright jerseys waiting their turn; boats run full and the swan boats sell out by mid-morning.
lore.when: place: hk_ashi; festival: koyo or goldenweek

lore.content: The university relay from Tokyo ends its first day here: the first runners come down the lakeside road around noon, towels on their shoulders, while old men with flags and runners' friends line the shore. The mountain leg is called the Mountain God's section.
Mist lies on the lake and the gate stands alone; the shore belongs to joggers, a few photographers with tripods and an old man who bows to the water.
Snow falls on dark water and the cedars; the boats stop for wind, and only swans and a few couples in heavy coats walk the shore.
They say that if Mt. Fuji is clear and mirrored in the lake at dawn, whatever someone starts that day will turn out well.

Ōwakudani is the scar of the last eruption of Mt. Hakone, about three thousand years ago: a valley of steam vents and sulfur. Eggs are boiled in baskets in the hot springs, and the sulfur turns the shells black. Legend says each one adds seven years of life; they are sold five to a bag.

The ropeway has stopped and the valley is closed: a loudspeaker repeats the sulfur reading, buses replace the cabins, and people with breathing problems are told to stay away. Staff are polite, tired and unmoved.
Mt. Fuji stands over the valley, white and clear, and a company outing queues at the railing for a group photo; steam drifts across the mountain like a veil.
Steam hangs thick in the cold, and frost whitens the railings; the hot pool where the egg baskets sit looks like a bath nobody dares enter.
The shop is packed with day-trippers buying ten bags at a time and the ropeway cabins fill; staff hand out numbered tickets for the eggs.
The slopes beyond the steam glow red and gold, and the cabin windows are full of faces turned to the leaves.
lore.when: place: hk_owakudani; season: autumn; period: afternoon

lore.content: Locals say the eggs taste better a day later, cold from the fridge, and that the shop keeps the day-old ones at the back for people who ask.

The Kirigaoka Sculpture Garden is an open-air sculpture garden on a Hakone hillside: The Reed Orchard (steel reeds that ring in the wind), Two Chairs (a bronze pair facing each other), The Hollow Giant (visitors can stand inside) and Rain Bowl. A small bronze frog is hidden among the ferns; the guides give no hints.
The maples around the sculptures are red and the bronze figures glow in the leaves; couples take photographs through the branches and the café terrace has a line.
Snow lies on the hollow giant's shoulders, the reeds ring with thin ice, and the café's windows steam; visitors walk quickly, bundled in coats, and linger at the terrace.
The hillside is nearly empty: a guide dozing on a stool, the reeds ringing for nobody, an art student alone in front of the giant.
lore.when: place: hk_sculpture; weekend: no; period: afternoon

lore.content: The hillside is fresh green and cedar pollen drifts; the lawn smells of cut grass and visitors sneeze quietly into handkerchiefs.
Rain beads on the steel and fills Rain Bowl, the only day it works as its maker intended; guides lend paper umbrellas at the gate.

Shizuka sometimes spends her morning off on one of Two Chairs, in jeans, looking at the empty one. Asked, she says it is the only place on the hill where nobody is waiting for her to answer a question.
lore.when: place: hk_sculpture; present: Shizuka; feels: Shizuka friend

lore.content: They say one of the steel reeds in The Reed Orchard is tuned a half-note flat on purpose, and the guides will point it out if asked nicely.
He knows Nanami has had a string of rebound flings since the breakup, and says nothing.
Since the breakup she has had a string of rebound flings; Ren knows and says nothing.

Her web novels are racy romances; she writes them at night at home and keeps the pen name from everyone at the shrine. She is shy about it in person, and the AI should not describe the novels' contents.

For her "research" she goes on dating-app dates under a fake name, never in Yanaka. The unknown illustrator whose online art she loves (Kanon) and she admire each other's work without knowing who the other is.

Once a month she secretly books Kaname (Shōta) at Club Eternal; he is the only person she talks to about the pressure. She goes for company and conversation; anything beyond is left to the player's AI.
She and Shizuka are a couple, secret from Shizuka's family; they steal time together on Shizuka's days off.
A host keeps clients company: pouring drinks, flattering, selling bottles for a commission. Some of the work is the performance of romance, and some of it spills past closing time.
His style is open and nothing with Lisa is exclusive.
Reiko is his monthly client, in secret; he treats her like any client who needs to talk, keeps her visits private, and never mentions her at work.

She was head hostess at Lounge Velvet, and years of hostess-club work in Kabukichō taught her how that world runs: bottles, debts, loyalty and loneliness. She talks about it plainly, with no illusions and no romance.

She has two younger lovers who don't know about each other, and she sees nothing wrong with it; neither has been promised anything. She keeps them apart with different nights and never at the bar. Airi drinks at her bar because Kyōko never asks about her work.
She bought Kanon's book at the summer fan convention, and doesn't say what is in it.
Pole dancing at Pole Star is a show: athletic, tipped, clients watch and don't touch.
Her style is open; her thing with Shōta is casual and neither expects more.
Momo takes her pole-fitness class.
A hostess club sells company and conversation: sofas, bottles, flattery. She protects her hostesses and keeps the line where she can, but the debt is squeezing her.
She says what she wants the night she wants it, plainly and without games, and expects the same back.
She and Rina are a couple, secret from her family.
Her style is open: she keeps things honest with whoever she is seeing and has no wish to be exclusive.

She draws adult doujinshi and is obsessed with eroge; she is a professional-minded adult about it and not ashamed. Yui's web novels are her favorite online writing, and she doesn't know who "Moon Fox" is (Yui admires her art in the same way).
Her work is as an AV actress: contracts, shoots away from any map, fans at signing events, the stigma. All of it is off-screen.
Her style is open, and she says what she wants.
She works as an AV actress: contracts, shoots away from any map, the stigma, the fear of her family finding out. All of it is off-screen.

places.name: Scramble Crossing & Hachikō
places.desc: the famous crossing under giant screens, and beside it a bronze dog on a stone plinth where half of Tokyo says "meet at Hachikō"
places.staff: crowds in every direction, station staff with whistles, buskers, people checking phones under the dog, tourists filming from the corners

places.name: Center Gai
places.desc: a pedestrian street of arcades, cheap food and neon signs: karaoke touts in the doorways, a noodle counter every ten steps, delivery bikes parked where it meets the crossing
places.staff: touts in black jackets, arcade clerks, noodle cooks, flyer handers, delivery riders waiting on their bikes by the gate

places.name: Golden Reel
places.desc: a loud pachinko parlor off Center Gai: rows of machines with spinning lights, steel balls roaring into trays, a prize counter at the back and a corner of old machines
places.staff: attendants in vests carrying trays of balls, a prize-counter clerk, night-shift workers and tired office workers staring at glowing machines

places.name: Echo Box Shibuya
places.desc: a ten-floor karaoke tower with a neon front, lobby touchscreens and corridors of padded private rooms; a drink bar on every floor and a night staff who have heard every song
places.staff: a front-desk clerk with a timer, room attendants with trays, office groups in the corridors, muffled singing behind every door

places.name: Hikari Labs
places.desc: two floors of a glass tower: standing desks in rows, whiteboards of half-erased plans, a kitchen with free snacks and a corner of beanbags that gets used more than it should
places.staff: engineers in headphones, a designer on a call, an intern carrying coffee, a courier handing over boxes at the door

places.name: Hello Bridge English
places.desc: a bright school on the third floor above a drugstore: small lesson booths with whiteboards, a lounge with coffee and flyers, and a counter clerk who greets everyone with a bow
places.staff: a counter clerk in a neat uniform, teachers from several countries between lessons, adult learners clutching workbooks

places.name: Takeshita Street
places.desc: a 350-meter lane of crêpe stands, costume shops, accessory stalls and photo booths with pop music from every doorway, always shoulder to shoulder and closed to cars
places.staff: crêpe cooks flipping batter, clerks in outrageous outfits calling out, a street photographer, university students and tourists sharing cotton candy

places.name: Omotesandō
places.desc: a wide avenue under zelkova trees: glass-fronted boutiques, hair salons on the upper floors and calm cafés in the back lanes, models carrying shopping bags
places.staff: boutique doormen, stylists on a smoke break, well-dressed shoppers, a photographer shooting a model by the trees, café waiters

places.name: Meiji Jingū
places.desc: a vast planted forest with a gravel path under a giant wooden torii; barrels of sake and wine line the way to a quiet main hall of cypress
places.staff: white-robed priests sweeping gravel, shrine maidens at the amulet office, visitors bowing at the torii, a few foreign tourists

places.name: Yoyogi Park
places.desc: wide lawns, cherry trees and a ginkgo avenue beside the forest: dancers at the gate on Sundays, flea-market tarps, joggers, dog walkers and bands rehearsing under the trees
places.staff: rockabilly dancers in leather and pompadours, joggers, dog walkers, a band rehearsing, flea-market sellers on blue tarps

places.name: Hotel Coco Palace, Dōgenzaka
places.desc: a pastel-lit hotel on the hill behind Center Gai, with an anonymous entrance, a panel of lit room photos in the lobby and a small window where the clerk speaks but is never seen
places.staff: a clerk watching a screen and speaking through the window, cleaners with carts, couples who don't meet anyone's eyes

places.name: Shinjuku Station
places.desc: the busiest station on Earth: two hundred exits, rivers of commuters, boarding jingles, underground arcades, towers on the west side and neon on the east
places.staff: attendants in white gloves pointing the way; commuters in streams; a bento kiosk; a busker by the south exit

places.name: Kabukichō
places.desc: the nightlife quarter under the giant red neon gate: touts in black coats, host portraits above every stairwell, pachinko roar spilling from every door, and streets lit brighter than noon
places.staff: touts with quotas; hosts and hostesses heading to work; delivery riders; neighborhood patrols in vests; crows at the garbage

places.name: Club Eternal
places.desc: a host club behind a black glass door: portrait boards of smiling men in suits out front; inside mirrors, chandeliers, deep sofas and champagne calls that stop the room
places.staff: hosts in dark suits rotating between tables; a floor captain; a doorman; women guests alone or in pairs

places.name: Lounge Velvet
places.desc: a hostess lounge on a fourth floor: low lights, deep sofas, bottles with name tags on the shelves, hostesses in evening dresses pouring drinks for company men
places.staff: hostesses in evening dresses; the mama circulating between tables; a bartender; company men in loosened ties

places.name: Omoide Yokochō
places.desc: a smoky alley of yakitori counters and tiny izakaya wedged by the train tracks: charcoal haze, elbows touching, and the whole row shaking when a train passes overhead
places.staff: cooks fanning charcoal; an old mama pouring beer; salarymen shoulder to shoulder; a few tourists with maps; trains overhead

places.name: Bar Kotori, Golden Gai
places.desc: a six-seat bar behind a narrow door in Golden Gai: a worn counter, a shelf of marked bottles, a karaoke machine older than the staff, and Mama pouring until dawn
places.staff: a young barback; regulars on the same stools every night; a retired editor second from the end; the karaoke book

places.name: Bar Lilac, Ni-chōme
places.desc: a bar up a narrow stair in Ni-chōme: warm lamps, a long counter and two sofas, mismatched chairs, a shelf of board games, and friends, couples and people who just wanted a quiet drink
places.staff: the bartender, forties, who never asks a question and always notices; friends helping behind the counter; regulars of every kind

places.name: Metropolitan Government Observatory
places.desc: the free observation deck on the 45th floor of the twin-towered city hall: 202 meters up, all of Tokyo spread out under glass, Mt. Fuji on clear winter mornings, a shop at the end
places.staff: uniformed guides at the lift; security checking bags; a university hiking club in matching jackets; couples at the glass; a shop clerk

places.name: Shinjuku Gyoen
places.desc: the national garden: wide lawns, a French formal garden, a Japanese garden with a teahouse pond, a tropical greenhouse and a thousand cherry trees; no alcohol, a small gate fee, closed at sunset
places.staff: gate attendants selling tickets; gardeners raking; picnickers on sheets; elderly strollers; university students sketching

places.name: Nest Capsule Shinjuku
places.desc: a capsule hotel above a noodle shop: stacks of screened sleeping cubbies, lockers for shoes and suits, a communal bath and a vending-machine lounge, built for missed last trains
places.staff: a night clerk at a narrow desk; salarymen in borrowed pajamas; a cleaner mopping the baths; a backpacker

places.name: Shimokitazawa lanes
